This study explores the well-posedness of hyperbolic partial differential equations with time-dependent coefficients that decrease at a rate slower than logarithmic, but faster than polynomial, in terms of non-integral powers. A new estimate is established, allowing for the application of a method similar to the Strachan alternative and Beyer-Brezis Bocchi's fixed point theorem. This yields proof of global existence for first-order equations with certain loss of derivatives, and for second-order equations with minimal loss of derivatives. A corresponding result for the Cauchy problem of a particular first-order quasilinear equation is also demonstrated. This extends existing research into the realm of sublogarithmic coefficients, and approaches the logarithmic threshold from the polynomial side. Furthermore, it is revealed that for certain types of superlogarithmic coefficients, smoothing effect holds true, marking a significant advancement beyond current knowledge. This result is contingent upon an additional assumption regarding the decay rate of the coefficients in space, which can be satisfied by various types of anisotropic scales, including those involving logarithmic or polynomial rates. An example illustrating a scenario in which this assumption is satisfied is provided. Through the application of a conjugate operator technique, it is shown that for certain types of superlogarithmic right-hand side expressions, a related equation lacks a classical solution, but demonstrates a smoothing effect at a very slow rate, exceeding previously documented cases. This phenomenon is exemplified through an example involving a specific function, highlighting its significance and complexity. Lastly, a corresponding result for the corresponding first-order quasilinear equation is demonstrated, which can be applied to various types of functions, including those characterized by rapidly decreasing, step-like, oscillating, and other unique behaviors. These examples serve to further contextualize the problem at hand, shedding light on the influence of the right-hand side expression and initial data on the solution's behavior. Specifically, it is shown that solution converges to a particular nonlinear smoothing operator applied to the right-hand side expression as time approaches infinity, which can be either continuously or discontinuously connected to a particular set, depending on initial data conditions. These examples underscore the intricate interplay between right-hand side expression behavior, initial data, and solution properties at both the local and global scales, particularly in scenarios where the right-hand side expression exhibits complex, oscillating, and other unique behaviors. This research proposes a novel method to tackle Japanese term segmentation using a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, where the character-based approach employed in many existing models is replaced with a byte-based technique to enhance efficiency. Since byte-based models can mistakenly combine unrelated characters due to the orthographic nature of Japanese, a special "null" byte is introduced to address this issue. Additionally, this model incorporates a naming component and a semantic similarity metric optimized using a smoothed version of the NLP Toolbox's wiktionary dataset to capture Japanese word meanings. The model's performance is evaluated using the Japanese NLP (NINJA) dataset and the CoNLL 2003 English dataset for comparison, revealing that it achieves an 87.67% accuracy on NINJA. Notably, when trained over a period of 10 days as suggested by the NINJA rules, this model demonstrates superior performance with a 3% advantage over the top-performing English LSTM model. Moreover, by utilizing character-level LSTM models in conjunction with byte-based models, this approach emerges as the top performer on NINJA with an 87.67% accuracy. Utilizing character-level models alone yields an 86.52% accuracy, underscoring the efficacy of the proposed byte-based technique. Furthermore, this paper showcases the effectiveness of the LSTM model in terms of processing speed by highlighting that its 10-day trained version can correctly segment 88.35 Japanese characters (with 1 error per 1000 characters) in 0.000013 seconds. Users of Stack Overflow often need help from others regarding external link references that are either broken or no longer relevant. To enhance understanding and share knowledge effectively, it's essential to present relevant, working links to others, making it necessary to research popular external links shared within Stack Overflow context. To tackle issues arising from external links, such as broken ones, this research investigates frequently shared external links on Stack Overflow to understand how users present and share this information. The study aims to identify trends, patterns, and the effectiveness of presented links using various methods, including categorization, common external platforms, and link validation. The findings reveal that while users intend to share useful information, a high percentage of links are broken, mainly due to website rebranding or domain changes. To aid other users and shared knowledge, this research provides guidelines on presenting external links effectively. Furthermore, the study's data, including link mappings and associated tags, is made available for others to build upon. Potential future directions for research have also been identified. Galaxies come in various shapes and sizes due to their diverse distribution, 
which poses a problem for models trying to explain their formation and variation.
Current galaxy models face a "complexity crisis," as they often simplify 
galaxies into uniform forms, neglecting their inherent diversity, yet this
diversity likely stems from the complex formation processes that models aim to 
replicate. We examine the potential role of supermassive black holes in this
diversity, as they can create clumps of stars through their gravitational effect
even in the presence of a uniform initial galaxy setup. Using the Niels Bohr
Institute's PAMMINO code, we simulate a range of galaxy forms by varying the
strength of black hole interaction, from weak to intense, which in intense cases
leads to a dispersion similar to that observed in elliptical galaxies.
Furthermore, we explore the possibility of supermassive black holes as the 
cause of various unique spiral galaxy patterns, as well as the origin of a 
recently discovered vast spiral structure in our own Milky Way. Our research 
has significant implications for numerous black hole-galaxy mass estimates, 
as it suggests that numerous spiral galaxies may harbor unaccounted-for massive 
black holes, particularly those that exhibit a tight spiral pattern. 
Ultimately, we conclude that supermassive black holes have the potential to 
be the long-sought "galaxy diversity engine." Unfortunately, due to our 
limited computational capabilities, our research could be expanded upon, 
especially through utilizing more powerful supercomputers, such as those at 
Riken, Japan. We expect future research to further establish the supermassive 
black hole's role in creating galaxy diversity. We hope this research will lead

To combat climate change, nations must cooperate and implement policies reflected in the Paris Agreement, requiring efficient global climate governance. Yet, the intricate network of climate-related organizations and projects obstruct seamless cooperation and project implementation due to a lack of relevant information. Our Climate Knowledge Base addresses this challenge by supplying context-specific knowledge about climate-related projects and organizations. Our system is centered on a large graph database, facilitating the understanding and relationships between projects and initiatives. Our solution includes a web-based search engine and a workflow management system to guide policy analysts through relevant projects, organizations, and actions, as demonstrated in our case studies. Our Climate Knowledge Base is an open-source resource, available on GitHub, to ensure a high level of customizability for users. We believe this system can enhance climate cooperation and project implementation by providing valuable insights to global climate practitioners. Our climate knowledge base was utilized in a study's findings, which show that climate change mitigation projects are beneficial but lack execution due to a lack of information about existing projects, organizations, and funding opportunities. Our analysis also reveals that climate projects face common challenges and most projects are beneficial despite a lack of relevant information which hinders their implementation. We identified "climate change" as a primary topic and the top five relevant organizations and projects, as well as their connections and associated assets. Our research was grounded in our development of the Climate Knowledge Base, a semantic graph database technology. We hope this system will contribute to global climate governance by powering climate dialogue with a knowledge base. Our Climate Knowledge Base can be repurposed for other domains, such as biomedical research, where a similar lack of context and information may obstruct scientific progress. We envision this system to evolve into a platform for (semi-)automatic climate knowledge discovery, enabling researchers to identify and analyze latent patterns and relationships within our climate knowledge base. Our Climate Knowledge Base could also be developed into a recommendation system, suggesting relevant projects, organizations, and actions to global climate practitioners based on our graph database. Our Climate Knowledge Base could also be developed into a text analytics tool, extracting and aggregating climate-related information from unstructured text sources. We plan to open-source our project on GitHub, so it can be customized and applied in other domains, such as the biomedical research domain. We plan to extend our climate knowledge base with more context-specific knowledge, such as climate-related actions, events, and locations. Clinical symptoms recorded in patient notes hold significant value for informing and shaping diagnoses, yet their detailed description is often fragmented and implicit within clinical documents. Current systems face substantial challenges in extracting symptoms from unstructured clinical notes due to their ambiguous representation. To address this issue, we developed SymptomLink, a natural language processing model that uses a link prediction task to link patient symptoms with underlying diseases. However, the model's accuracy is limited by data restrictions and biases, particularly in the lack of data on certain symptoms and their relationships with diseases. To overcome these limitations, we applied a data augmentation technique that utilises unlinked data, effectively enhancing the model's performance across different domains. In experiments using the MIMIC-III clinical dataset, we demonstrated that the proposed method achieves a 9.4 F1 score in symptom event extraction, outperforming existing models by 4.8 F1 score points. Notably, the model exhibits strong generalizability, with its F1 score improving by 5.8 points in an unsupervised domain adaptation setting and 3.4 points in a domain generalization setting. The proposed approach thus offers a promising solution for extracting symptoms from clinical notes while mitigating data-related biases and limitations. Despite significant progress, the technical hurdles for fully self-sustaining vehicles remain, particularly in accurately interpreting and responding to environmental cues. This project tackles the autonomous navigation challenge by developing a Deep Reinforcement Learning framework that enables an autonomous vehicle to safely and efficiently traverse new routes while avoiding obstacles. Finally, we outline potential future research directions that could bring fully autonomous driving within reach. Our study examines how current computing infrastructure affects personal assistant usage. We developed Pando, a browser-based Personal Assistant Computing system, to examine the impact of underlying technology. We conducted a user study comparing Pando to Google Assistant, analyzing averse behavior and how it influences Pando's usability. We found that Pando induces significantly less frustration than Google Assistant, but does not improve task completion or interaction ease. The discrepancy reveals that latent system issues affecting performance can be hidden by a seamless user interface, highlighting the importance of considering the role of underlying technology in shaping personal assistant design. We obtained ethical approval for this study from our institution.

This research focuses on estimating the highest eigenvalue and corresponding eigenvector of a nonlinear operator based on noisy data, which can be represented as an eigenvalue problem for an incomplete nonlinear matrix after partial pertication. It introduces a new estimation approach, involving an iterative minimization of a discrete transformation matrix with constrained rational structure. This method is proven to converge optimally in frequency domain and converges converges at a rate of O(1/n) in expectation when estimating the eigenvalue, matching the best possible convergence rate, while also achieving the best possible convergence rate for the eigenvector under certain conditions. Notably, this result holds even when the operator is highly irregular, with its smoothness much lower than the dimensions of the involved matrices. Furthermore, this research is the first to estimate nonlinear eigenproblems even in cases where the operator is highly irregular, with significantly better performance than previous methods that have specific smoothness constraints. Finally, a study was conducted to evaluate the performance of this research using simulated data. It demonstrated that the estimated eigenvalue and eigenvector converge rapidly as the signal-to-noise ratio increases. Additionally, the eigenvalue estimates were found to be consistent and converge rapidly even when the operator is highly irregular, matching closely with the actual values despite being highly irregular. Finally, this research was compared with existing estimation methods, revealing that it significantly outperforms these methods in various tests. This research opens up several avenues for further investigation, including extending its results to estimate multiple eigenvalues, developing novel applications using the estimated eigenvalue and eigenvector, and enhancing the structure of the rational matrix model using machine learning techniques. We examine low-complexity sequences produced by the greedy transformation associated with a two-dimensional Sierpinski triangle grid and show that they share significant parallels with sequences generated by the intermediate $\beta$-shifts, a class of sequences we previously studied, by demonstrating a analogous relationship. This connection enables us to recharacterize the ergodicity and braking phenomena observed in the intermediate $\beta$-shifts through the established links with the greedy transformation, thereby broadening our understanding of these phenomena. We also point out that the proven results for the greedy maps can be utilized to derive new insights into the intermediate $\beta$-shifts, effectively transferring knowledge between these sequences. Consequently, the terminology used to describe the nonergodic cases is modified to "braking with a gap", reflecting the discovered parallels, and we establish that sequences produced by the greedy transformation are in one-to-one correspondence with those generated by the intermediate $\beta$-shifts, thereby solidifying the previously observed similarities between these sequences. Moreover, we derive upper limits on the Hausdorff dimension of the set where sequences produced by the greedy transformation exhibit braking behavior and demonstrate that these limits are attainable, thus providing a more detailed characterization of this set's properties. We also explore connections between the Hausdorff dimension of the set where sequences produced by the greedy transformation exhibit braking behavior and the Kolmogorov complexity of the associated sequences, by showing that the dimension of this set is linked to the maximum Kullback-Leibler divergence associated with the greedy maps and is thus greater than zero, a result which can be extended to the sequences produced by the intermediate $\beta$-shifts, thereby broadening our understanding of the relationship between the sequences' complexity and their braking behavior. We also point out that the established links between the greedy transformation and the intermediate $\beta$-shifts can be generalized to various models based on different grids, thereby facilitating a more universal characterization of the sequences' properties. We also examine whether similar results can be derived for the higher-order $\beta$-shifts and explore connections between the sequences' properties and the associated parameters, thereby providing a more detailed understanding of these sequences' dynamic behavior. We also point out that the studied results can be extended to various models based on different grids and provide a more general characterization of the sequences' properties, by showing that the greedy maps can be utilized to derive upper limits on the Hausdorff dimension of the set where sequences produced by the beta-transformation exhibit braking behavior.

We've found that a $SO(N_c)$ gauge theory can be represented by an arrangement of Dirac fermions with no fermion irreducible representations, allowing for an interplay between fermions in fermi surfaces and those in fermi bubbles. In this context, we present a model involving $N_f=N_s+2$ fermi surfaces, demonstrating that the theory can be in a phase where fermi surfaces are completely enclosed by fermi bubbles for $N_s \geq 2$. This model also includes an additional term that slightly breaks chiral symmetry and is proportional to a very small number $\epsilon$. As the charge of the fermions in the fermi surfaces exceeds 1, the regime where fermi surfaces are completely enclosed by fermi bubbles expands into a region that includes the entire parameter space of the theory for small values of $\epsilon$. In this same regime, the concept of confinement in the theory's $SO(N_c)$ gauge symmetry holds true. Additionally, the relationships between gauge symmetry, bosonization, chiral symmetry breaking, and charge ordering that were discovered in a one-dimensional $SU(N_c)$ Kondo lattice model continue to apply here, particularly with the emergence of a magnon-fermion liquid state that exhibits charge density waves when $N_s=2$. A notable property of this model lies in its set of interquark potential energy curves that, due to charge ordering in fermi surfaces, become Dirac matrices polarized by the effects of $\epsilon$ and mass scales of the theory that are much larger in scale. Finally, we present a description of infrared properties in a related $SO(N_c, N_{\text{right}})$ gauge theory that can be used to describe non-Abelian anyons in systems with medium spin. In this theory, which features $N_f= N_s +2$ fermi surfaces, we've discovered a region in parameter space where fermi surfaces are completely enclosed by fermi bubbles for $N_s \geq 2$, and it's here that the concept of charge ordering in fermi surfaces ferromagnetically aligns with each other. Furthermore, this model contains not just Dirac monopoles but also 't Hooft polynomials, and related polyloops in a polarized state induced by $\epsilon$ and much larger scale monopole couplings that are present in the theory's set of multivalued gauge potentials. Machine learning models, notably random forests, have become widely utilized due to their exceptional performance and minimalistic simplicity in the AI community. However,  deep learning models have increasingly gained preference over random forests due to their better performance, despite certain challenges that arise from their opacity. In contrast, the internal workings of random forests are relatively easy to comprehend, which presents an opportunity to utilize feature importance as a clear and accessible means of model interpretation. 

This study introduces a novel, clear, and accessible means of interpreting random forest and enhanced tree models beyond traditional feature importance, yielding a detailed breakdown of how target values are predicted based on model input. A clear and interpretable method is derived for enhanced neural networks through comparison with their equivalent model architectures under supernet settings. Moreover, this study enhances existing model interpretation methods by facilitating the attribution of prediction variations to specific input features, which has previously been a contentious issue. 

The proposed framework consists of three primary components. Firstly, it demarcates the internal model structures that contribute to target prediction, which is relatively straightforward in enhanced tree models but requires comparison of different model structures in supernet settings. Secondly, it defines the scope of model parameters that govern prediction variations, which is simply the structure itself in enhanced tree models but needs to be compared with numerous candidate structures in supernet settings. Thirdly, it quantifies the importance of different input features by tracing back their impact on prediction variations, which is relatively straightforward in model structures and supernet settings. 

The experimental outcomes reveal that this study's framework yields clearer and more accessible model interpretation outcomes across multiple regression and classification datasets. The outcome also shows that enhanced tree models yield comparable performance to state-of-the-art neural networks, which presents a significant breakthrough in terms of model interpretation.

In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, participating parties and their data remain vulnerable to potential threats, such as jurisdictional overlaps with hostile entities. To address these risks, we propose establishing a federated framework within multiple Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), each hosting a participant's data, to safeguard against hardware and software attacks. This innovative approach, flatee, allows for secure model training across these TEEs, separate from the participants' actual data, by employing remote execution and hardware-based isolation. Specifically, our prototype utilizes Intel Software Guard Extensions (SGX) to create and manage distinct TEEnvironments, where participants can train models with consistency, using protocols adapted from the federated learning paradigm. Notably, results show that even with semi-smooth objectives and Byzantine attacks, combining stochastic gradient averaging with a robust top-k filtering strategy leads to consistent performance, with only minor discrepancies, across multiple runs. Furthermore, our implementation achieves a remarkable 94% performance gain, in comparison to a single-TEE setup using SGX. This groundbreaking work brings federated learning into TEEs, separate from actual data, thus safeguarding against hardware and software attacks. With potential applications across various domains, this innovative approach represents a significant advancement, protecting participants and their sensitive data from potential threats. This research introduces Timeloops, a component that automatically generates system call policies for containerized microservices based on dynamic analysis. Containing a microservice within a container enhances system consistency by restricting access to certain system resources but fails to provide same-level network and process isolation. Thus, there's a need for supplementary security mechanisms, such as access control, especially for sensitive resources like file systems and network connections. Drawn from the literature, examples of system call policies for various microservices like HTTP servers, databases, and file servers reveal the complexity involved in manually defining these policies due to the diverse nature of microservices.

However, manually crafting system call policies for microservices is labor-intensive and prone to errors. Moreover, as microservices evolve over time, their system call patterns change, necessitating periodic policy updates via manual redefinition, which can lead to policy inconsistencies and security vulnerabilities. In contrast, Timeloops leverages runtime system call tracing and learning to create and evolve system call policies in real-time, starting from an initial training phase for each microservice type. Furthermore, Timeloops is designed as a scalable, lightweight, and component-based framework that's easily integratable into existing containers. The results of various functional tests confirm the efficacy and accuracy of Timeloops in generating system call policies for microservices. The main contributions of Timeloops are its novel learning approach and its component-based design, which distinguish it from other related systems. Ultimately, Timeloops provides a simple, effective, and efficient means of automatically generating system call policies for containerized microservices. Merchandise space, a type of structured database, represents entities and their connections between various categories through partial order relationships. Our research builds upon this concept, specifically exploring linear classification models within a framework known as Linear Experiments over Directed Acyclic Graphs (LEXDAGs), which was first introduced by Belahlid et al. in 2020. By combining linear classification with the merchandise space structure, we can identify subsets of relevant attributes and reduce dimensionality, resulting in improved data interpretation and computational efficiency. Our theoretical analysis examines the convergence of LexDAG-based linear classification and reveals a relationship between attribute selection and region partitioning in merchandise space. Additionally, we illustrate the efficacy of our approach using real-world data sets, showcasing enhanced data interpretation and performance outcomes. Our results demonstrate that linear classification in this structured environment leads to better generalization, accurate attribute identification, and optimal classification performance. Our methodology can be applied to various domains involving directed acyclic graphs, such as biology and computer vision, to identify effective attribute subsets for linear classification. This introduction focuses on developing and implementing Random Model Predictive Control (MPC) algorithms to solve complex optimization problems that arise in control systems. A detailed example illustrates the main steps of designing and implementing an MPC algorithm, with particular attention to computational efficiency to handle high-dimensional problems, (pseudo)random constraints, and real-time processing needs. Key concepts underlying Random MPC are outlined, along with the current state of related research in the field. The associated software and technical details are accessible through public repositories as mentioned in Section 13.2. Moreover, demo videos showcasing the Random MPC method on flying robots are available on YouTube. Please refer to Section 13.2 for more information regarding software access and YouTube demo links. 

In this chapter, we aim to provide an in-depth introduction to Random MPC by exemplifying its development and implementation in a control problem. A comprehensive mathematical representation of a quadcopter's dynamics is used to demonstrate the application of Random MPC in a complex state space scenario. The algorithm is designed to generate optimal control inputs by minimizing a cost function that takes into account state constraints, input limits, and a penalty term for control effort. To enhance computational efficiency, we leverage (i) sparse optimization techniques, (ii) active set methods, and (iii) Bonsor's algorithm. The resulting algorithm is capable of processing up to 200-300 variables in each iteration. Furthermore, we incorporate numerical perturbations to system inputs to enhance robustness against unknown disturbances, (pseudo)random state constraints to account for uncertainty in state estimates, and introduce a novel penalty term for controlling the variability in input commands. To accelerate processing, we eliminate non-essential variables from the optimization problem through a sensitivity analysis, resulting in a significant reduction in computational requirements. The proposed algorithm is demonstrated to outperform predictive control methods without randomization, input variability penalization, and robust state estimation. Moreover, we showcase its implementation on a flying robot quadcopter using demo videos and publicly accessible software as detailed in Section 13.2.

This research centers around developing methods to analyze large, high-dimensional datasets, specifically via Singular Component Analysis (SCA), where we capture essential subspace variations through a few key singular components. To tackle the limitations imposed by the immense size of these datasets, we leverage compressive sensing (CS) techniques to create a CS-SCA framework, where a reduced number of informative measurements are taken into account. This enables the accurate recovery of SCs from an under-determined system, facilitated by a few CS-sampled dataset snapshot. Theoretical underpinnings for SC recovery are established using deterministic analysis and asymptotic spike-configuration results, confirming the effectiveness of our approach. To demonstrate its value, we apply CS-SCA to the analysis of massive genomic, network traffic, and image data. Moreover, a novel compressive SCA-based streaming algorithm is proposed, allowing for real-time subspace analysis of streaming data, with accompanying theoretical guarantees for accurate SC recovery. Experimental results validate the efficacy of our methods, showcasing their superiority over traditional approaches. This method initially obtains a plot of the minimal preliminary model, created by combining one-dimensional subspaces of the normalized fiber ring's valuation semigroup, which are extracted through a constructive process. Our analysis includes a detailed examination of the case of one-dimensional local rings with mixed characteristic, and we demonstrate the efficacy of this approach via a substantial number of illustrative examples. Additionally, we have successfully applied this algorithm to derive a constructive proof of the Neron desingularization for one-dimensional valuation domains. This research not only offers a practical solution but also identifies and responds to previously unresolved problems, specifically addressing the applicability of Neron desingularization in low-dimensional settings and the feasibility of constructing valuation domains through graph analysis. Our evidence shows that this expanded framework reaches the boundary of $\mathsf{PSO}$ within two variables and reaches the boundary of monotone $\mathsf{PSO}$ with one variable, while remaining at the second level of the arithmetic hierarchy for two variables. Our new sets of sentences build upon the'small' and'medium' classes introduced by Wilkie-Zhuk and Stepanik, showcasing a unified approach to expressing these classes within first-order logic. This study determines the exponential count of random walk locations within a $d$-dimensional integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ by using the $L_1$-norm distance with a radius of $R$. By transforming this problem into a combinatorial issue involving partitions of integers $3R+1$, we derive an asymptotic formula for the exponential count and establish that it grows with the function $e^{R\sqrt{d\log R}}$ as $d$ approaches infinity. This result is compared to the known $e^{R\frac{1}{\sqrt{18\pi}}\sqrt{d}}$ from previous works and justified by the central limit theorem. Furthermore, we show that the desired exponential count can be calculated efficiently using a dynamic programming approach that runs in $O(R^3)$ time. This leads to an interesting open problem of determining if it's possible to achieve an $O(R^2)$ time complexity for this calculation. Finally, we conduct several experiments to verify that the derived asymptotic formula accurately estimates the exponential count at least up to a radius of $R=200$. Due to certain limitations in our current approach, we are unable to test larger values of $R$ at this time. Consequently, we pose a conjecture that the derived asymptotic formula remains accurate for all positive integers $R$. Brian simulator models neuronal activity through detailed descriptions of neuron and synapse behavior, whereas this project translates that information into code compatible with the Clyde compiler, which compiles neural networks for execution on the neuromorphic chip Loihi. Additionally, we introduced a novel object-oriented extension to Clyde, allowing for a more natural translation of Brian code and enhancing the compiler's capabilities. Our simulator, Brian2Loihi, successfully emulates Brian networks on Loihi, demonstrating the feasibility of using Brian as a intermediate step between neural network designs and hardware implementations on Loihi. Moreover, we found that Brian2Loihi outperforms standard Clyde compilations, particularly in scenarios with many synthetic operations. However, we observed that high-performance compilation from Brian requires modifications to the compiler, particularly handling of variable naming discrepancies. Furthermore, we discovered potential issues with Brian's synthetic variable handling and neuron updates that could lead to incorrect simulation results, particularly with floating-point values and non-local connections. These potential issues could be resolved by utilizing Clyde's native variables or compiling them directly onto Loihi without intermediate synthetic constructs. Our work offers a solution for the "simulator problem" by providing a usable and tested intermediate step between neural network designs and hardware implementations on Loihi, while also highlighting areas for improvement in both Brian and Clyde. We hope this research will contribute to the development of more efficient and reliable neural network compilers for similar neuromorphic chips in the future. Additionally, the effect of rotational momentum is more pronounced in the outer regions of the accretion disk, leading to a biweight profile's growth being delayed relative to a Gaussian profile. This effect increases with rotational momentum and radial location, and diminishes as the accretion profile becomes thinner. We explore the phenomenon of electromagnetic radiation emitted by an atom when it moves towards a mirror, representing a more realistic scenario of cavity QED experiments. For a rapidly moving atom, the energy emitted can be attributed to the acceleration of its center of mass, rather than its electronic transitions. We establish that the radiation spectrum is a combination of the atom-mirror vacuum entanglement and the Dagom-Jaynes point-like source model. Additionally, the emission pattern is unaffected by the atom's internal electronic states. However, the absence of radiation in the dipole approximation indicates that the atom behaves as a massive particle, and the likelihood of spontaneous emission is linked to the atom-mirror entanglement. We also examine the potential for stimulated emission and find that, under certain conditions, the probability of stimulated emission exceeds that of spontaneous emission. The likelihood of stimulated emission increases as the atom's velocity in the direction of the mirror diminishes and the width of the mirror's opening becomes narrower. These findings provide valuable insights into the relationship between radiation and the atom-mirror interaction, shedding light on the entanglement phenomenon. Moreover, the probability of emitting two photons is primarily dependent on the two-atom-two-mirror interaction state and can be described as a product of the Hartley-Mandel condition and the atom-mirror entanglement. We also demonstrate that the probability distribution of emitted photons follows a Poisson distribution when the mirror is thin, resulting in a radiation spectrum characterized by a Lorentzian lineshape. This work offers a framework for understanding non-stationary atom-mirror interactions, linking radiation phenomena to cavity QED experiments, and potentially enabling the creation of ultra-low temperature non-equilibrium systems. Located approximately 15,000 light-years from Earth in the Narrow Waist of Carina, lies the young cluster, Westerlund 2 (WCL 2), which hosts a vast number of O stars and giant H II regions. Recently, an extensive study of WCL 2 revealed that the cluster is comprised of multiple subgroups with distinct colors, which are arranged in a north-south direction. Focusing on O stars in the western part of the cluster, particularly in the red color subgroup, researchers have identified three new Wolf-Rayet stars and eight new O stars using diverse spectroscopic techniques. Utilizing absolute magnitudes and deredshifted energies, a comprehensive analysis of the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram for the western stars was carried out, which led to the detection of two blue-straggler stars. One of the WR stars is confirmed to be a narrow-band emitter with a narrow band temperature of 3920-4050 K, which classifies it as a WN8 category. Two other WR stars show spectral characteristics similar to WR121B and WR124, which is a single, broad-band temperature of approximately 4000-6000 K. Additionally, two candidate Ofp/WNSe stars are detected, which exhibit both WR and O-star features, often associated with the late stage of nitrogen expansion in single WN stars. Further study is required to confirm the WR nature of two O stars identified as such. Three massive stellar content surveys in the region show inconsistent data regarding the presence of single WN7-9 stars in the area. It is proposed that a major stellar content disruption occurred about 500,000 years ago, which led to significant changes in the visible population of WCL 2, including a reduction in the single WN7-9 count. This event is believed to have corresponded to a relatively low star formation rate of 8 * 10^-5 M_solar_per_year. Two possible scenarios are presented to explain the observed mass disorder and reduced WR population, which include a random sampling and a stage preceding single WN7-9 in the single WN7-9 evolution branch. Furthermore, a random sampling could be linked to another mechanism, which is to attribute the mass disorder to a post-WR velocity kick. Two new variables, which could be key in understanding the mass disorder, are introduced in this paper: the fraction of single WN7-9s in the single WN7-9 branch and the average time before becoming a single WN7-9. This research presents a novel approach to improving handwritten documents by leveraging both traditional handwritten text reading and generation techniques. We developed an innovative model called HERT, comprising of two interconnected networks - a text generator and a text-guided adversarial network - designed to enhance scanned document images. Specifically, the text generator employs a CNN-LSTM model, which not only extracts text features from the images but also generates the reading through a decoder. The Universal Approximation Theorem states that any continuous function can be approximated by a neural network with a single hidden layer containing a sufficient number of hidden units. However, determining the optimal number of hidden units remains a challenging task. Typically, networks are constructed using the trial-and-error method by adjusting hyperparameters through backpropagation, but this can be computationally expensive. In response to this limitation, an alternative method is proposed here, where the number of hidden layers and the size of each layer, including the output layer, are automatically determined without the need for backpropagation. A key aspect of this approach is a novel theorem that establishes a relationship between neural networks and the covering of intervals, analogous to the Cantor Set construction. By leveraging this theorem, a systematic procedure is developed for constructing a neural network that can approximate any continuous function with a high degree of accuracy. Furthermore, the resulting neural network architecture is shown to be equivalent to a well-known class of networks, where each hidden unit has a nonlinear transfer function, and the connections between layers are fully connected. Moreover, an alternative implementation is provided where each hidden unit has a nonlinear input structure based on the original work of Kolmogorov, and the connections between layers are fully connected. This method enables the automatic determination of the number of hidden units, as well as the width of each layer, and can even handle cases where the input data is high-dimensional, and the output is multi-dimensional. Several numerical examples are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, and compared to other state-of-the-art neural network architectures, which require backpropagation for hyperparameter tuning. Despite its superiority, the method has a few limitations, and could only be proven theoretically for specific types of neural network architectures, and requires significant computational resources for high-dimensional data sets, and will be made available open-source. Based on these findings, two possible enhancements are proposed for future work. First, a more general implementation is needed that can be applied to a broader class of neural network architectures. Second, more efficient algorithms are needed to improve the computational efficiency of the method. Once these challenges are addressed, the method has the potential to become a leading approach for constructing neural networks based on the Universal Approximation Theorem. Until then, it will remain a valuable contribution that can be built upon by future research. In particular, it is worth noting that the method is not limited to approximation tasks, but can also be used for regression tasks and solving optimization problems, as long as the target function is continuous. When analyzing data, we often utilize the median absolute deviation as a robust measure of a dataset's central tendency variation. Unlike the typical variance, this measure is resistant to extreme outliers. However, when attempting to estimate the median absolute deviation with a limited number of samples, bias becomes a major concern, especially in large datasets. This paper proposes a family of asymptotically unbiased estimators for the median absolute deviation, which can be easily calculated using sample data. These estimators demonstrate improved performance over a commonly used biased estimator, particularly in extremely large datasets. Additionally, we examine the theoretical behavior of our proposed estimators and verify that they converge to the true value at a rate of O_n(-1/2n) on a subset of distribution functions known as the'smooth MAD functions.' This convergence is independent of the distribution's parameters, including the mean and variance. Notably, this rate is clogarithmic in the sample size, making it the best achievable outcome. To facilitate efficient estimation, we can approximate the true minimum by leveraging a variant of the Kullback-Leibler divergence. This method enables us to generate a confidence interval for the median absolute deviation using extremal order statistics, which exhibit an accelerated rate of convergence. Finally, we test the performance of our proposed estimators in a series of simulation studies, demonstrating their improved results compared to the commonly employed estimator. Moreover, this estimator outperforms existing alternatives in a range of scenarios, including the mean absolute deviation and the interquartile range estimators. All related software codes are available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/Estimation-MAD. This repository includes the necessary R code for reproducing the figures and performing the simulations. Furthermore, it includes a function for generating bias-corrected estimates of the median absolute deviation, which can be employed in future research and applications. This function is also compatible with parallel processing, enabling enhanced performance in large datasets. Specifically, the function 'bc_mad' can be used to generate the desired estimates, which must be input with the required parameters, including the number of samples (n), the significance level (alpha), and a minimum value for the estimated median absolute deviation (min.est). The task of Relation Extraction aims to extract information about the relationships between entities within a text. A key challenge in achieving high accuracy is the sparsity of labeled data, which makes it difficult to develop effective models. To overcome this limitation, we propose utilizing Knowledge Graph Embeddings as a complementary resource to improve Relation Extraction results. By framing this task as a two-stage process – first predicting knowledge graph links from relation triples, and then using extracted features to enhance the classification of relation triples in Relation Extraction – we demonstrate significant improvements in accuracy on three datasets. Notably, our method also facilitates the interpretation of models by highlighting crucial sentence features in relation extraction. Our study focused on the magnetic arrangements within the crystals of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 at various temperatures, examining their effects on the magnetic susceptibility and specific heat. Notably, the Ru bonds in these materials exhibit alternating patterns, resulting in unique internal magnetic fields at varying intensities. This distinct feature led to the realization of two ordered states, specifically ferromagnetic orders in Nd3RuO7 and a partially disordered state, denoted as "quasi-long range order" in 1217, at respective temperatures of 5.5 K and 18 K, specifically for Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7. This quasi-long range order in 1217 was attributed to growth of chain ordered domains, despite the presence of a disordering effect from 1217 bond. Furthermore, the discovery of a half-magnetization state in 1217 was also documented. Our examination of the magnetic arrangements within the crystals of Tb2+ exhibited the largest effect on the Ru magnetism, resulting in the observed quasi-long range order in 1217. Lastly, our examination of the specific heat failed to detect any magnetic phase transition in the entropy, instead revealing a continuous increase in the entropy at 18 K. This phenomenon can be attributed to the necessary conditions for a magnetic phase transition in 1217 being unfulfilled. In contrast to the expected third-law entropy at zero Kelvin, the measured entropy at zero Kelvin in 1217 was noticeably lower, specifically 0.34 J/mol K, instead of the third-law value of 1.07 J/mol K. In related studies, the same researchers discovered a similar partial disordered state in another material, denoted as KFe3(SO4)3Cl, possessing similar magnetic arrangements and 1217 bonds. The characteristics of a minimum are defined by a set of irreducible components originating from the materials' phonon modes.  The classification of these minima relies on grouping these components based on similarity and is not influenced by the manual ordering of components.  An automatic procedure is developed to identify the components and their corresponding mappings across different materials and phases, paving the way for the creation of comprehensive databases.  By analyzing a database of 1100 structures, it is observed that a minimum can remain unchanged across different phases for less frequently occurring symmetry types.  Additionally, it is found that certain transformations involving lattice rotation are linked to the materials' topological properties.  Notably, a minimum associated with the rotation symmetry in a hexagonal structure is found to be completely disconnected, resulting in a high energy barrier between different phases.  By utilizing a theoretical model based on this energy, it is possible to achieve a level of accuracy in predicting phase transition energies of around 10%.  These findings provide valuable insights into the connection between lattice structure and materials' behavior.  Also, the developed database presents numerous opportunities for further research, such as using machine learning algorithms to make predictions based on the collected data.  By combining experimental and theoretical techniques, it is possible to make new discoveries about materials' properties and create more effective technologies. Our study explores the influence of head-mounted display distortions on user experiences in immersive virtual environments. A novel instrument was developed to assess the severity of distortions and their impact on user satisfaction. Through a survey of 283 users, we examined the relationship between head-mounted display distortions and their effect on user experiences under various conditions. The results reveal that user ratings of distortion severity and satisfaction correlate with our instrument's measurements and remain consistent across different scenarios. However, satisfaction ratings are primarily determined by distortion severity, while user-related factors play a minor role. Furthermore, satisfaction ratings are consistently lower in environments that incorporate natural stimuli compared to binary stimuli. The findings provide valuable insights for VR application development, suggesting the importance of considering user perspectives on distortion severity to optimize experiences. Moreover, developers should prioritize addressing head-mounted display distortions to enhance user satisfaction, particularly in environments that incorporate natural stimuli. Finally, we demonstrate that user perspectives on distortion severity can differ from developer perspectives, highlighting potential best practices for the gaming industry. Based on our research, we have identified several potential areas of investigation for further study. Notably, CPT can easily distinguish graphs characterized by a single path or a linear structure with designated starting and ending points. Notably, PCDP's capabilities fall short even when attempting to solve a straightforward equation, such as $x+1=y$. This result has significant implications in algebraic geometry, suggesting the existence of distinct algebraic curves that can be accurately modeled using PCDP formulas. This discovery further reinforces existing research claiming that PCDPD has limited powers in resolving certain algebraic equations. A subring collection in a ring $R$, that is associative, commutative nor unital, is defined as $\sigma$-elementary when it meets a specific countable union criterion based on the ring's ideals. In this research, an endless family of commutative local rings with this $\sigma$-elementary subring collection is discovered, providing an endless variety of local rings with this collection. Furthermore, a relationship between these rings and countable linear local $\mathbb{Q}$-algebras is established, providing a second endless variety of such algebras with this collection. It was also demonstrated that not every non-commutative local ring with this collection is constructed from the union of its ideals and that this collection is distinct from the Gilmer-Harris collection. Lastly, a connection between this collection and Artinian rings is explored. Finally, several unanswered questions regarding this collection are presented. The term 'endless' refers to a countably infinite sequence, not a truly endless series.

We propose a new framework that verifies the reliability of Bayesian models by testing their performance on corrupted datasets and provides confidence intervals for their results. The framework is then applied to three common models, including the Gaussian process, neural networks with dropout, and the Gaussian process with data augmentation, and we show that verifying the reliability of these models is feasible. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the reliability of Bayesian models can be maintained when sampling from posterior distributions without introducing additional bias. Experimental studies confirm that the reliability of Bayesian models correlates positively with their credibility. The benefits of this framework emerge in tasks such as computer vision, where we demonstrate that the reliability of Bayesian models can be utilized to generate reliable uncertainty quantifications for predictions on images, and to conduct reliable evidence calculation for hypotheses based on these images. The COVID-19 pandemic is considered one of the most severe public health crises in history, exacerbated by online misinformation spread via social media platforms. In China, a strict "double line of defense" regulatory framework aims to control the dissemination of harmful information, with both government-censored and individual-generated content subject to suppression. Our study analyzes the impact of official efforts to combat online rumors, evaluating both the effectiveness of government-censored content and the influence of individual rumor-mongering. Utilizing data from Weibo, a popular Chinese micro-blogging platform, our research methodology involves the application of natural language processing techniques such as BERT to identify "online rumors" and their spread across different Chinese provinces. Our analysis reveals that both government-censored and individual-generated content have a significant impact on the dissemination of online rumors, with further examination showing that official suppression can actually accelerate the spread of censored information when the source is the government. Conversely, individual involvement appears to have a more subtle but persistent effect. Ultimately, our findings underscore the importance of understanding the dynamics of misinformation spread and the efficacy of regulatory measures to combat online rumors. Based on our research, we propose several avenues for further investigation. Specifically, we suggest exploring the causality between government suppression and the spread of censored information, as well as the potential differences in user behavior following supression by the government versus individual users. Additionally, we recommend conducting a more nuanced analysis of the counter-measures employed by the Chinese authorities to combat online rumors, as well as the perspectives of netizens regarding individual involvement in rumor-mongering. Lastly, we encourage researchers to extend our study by examining the impact of the double line of defense regulatory framework on education, taking into account the diverse range of keywords related to online rumors in this field. With these potential research directions in mind, our study seeks to contribute to the ongoing discussion on the spread of online rumors and misinformation, particularly in China, and the effectiveness of regulatory measures to combat them. Furthermore, we hope to shed light on the influence of individual involvement in rumor-mongering and the efficacy of government suppression. By leveraging advanced natural language processing techniques, we identified and analyzed online rumors and their spread across different Chinese provinces during the pandemic, as well as the impact of both government-censored and individual-generated content. This research investigates the effects of dimensionality reduction in hyperspectral image processing on classification accuracy using real-world data. Hyperspectral images, comprising numerous spectral bands, pose significant analysis challenges due to their high dimensionality. Various spectral dimensionality reduction methods have been developed to simplify data analysis by compressing redundant spectral information. However, the potential of these techniques is often underexplored in remote sensing applications. Focusing on the Hyperspectral Remote Sensing Challenge 2019 data set, this study assesses the classification performance of three machine learning models using different dimensionality reduction methods. An evaluation of the techniques' computational complexities and features is also conducted to identify remote sensing applicable methods. Our findings indicate that, depending on the dataset and parameters, feature selection can be a viable option for dimensionality reduction. Additionally, the study highlights the advantages and limitations of each method to guide the selection of spectral dimensionality reduction techniques in remote sensing applications. Compressing large language models with smaller, trained or randomly initialized models has gained traction as a means of reducing the models' massive computational and memory requirements. However, existing methods that employ compressed models in inference often lead to subpar performance compared to the original model, making them less feasible for practical use. Moreover, the problem of accurately measuring compressed models' efficacy is compounded by the model's state initialization, particularly when the initialized state differs greatly from the original model's state. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel metric for evaluating the compressed model's quality and propose a pioneering approach - the Pseudo-Parallel Decoding (PPD) method - that enables the effective utilization of compressed models in inference. Notably, the PPD method demonstrates superior performance across a range of language understanding tasks and outperforms current top methods in the field, achieving notable reductions in model size while achieving scores comparable to the original model. To further validate the method's efficacy, we conducted thorough examinations of the models' weight distribution during decoding and the convergence of the compressed models under repeated sampling of the model weights. Interestingly, our analysis reveals that the success of the PPD method can be attributed to the models' self-consistency, which is achieved through iterative inference, confirming the method's potential for widespread application. A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, enables fast and precise calculation of amide proton chemical shifts for proteins with any level of resolution, employing quantum mechanics. ProCS leverages a pre-trained quantum machine learning model and yields predictions within a timeframe of milliseconds per residue. Through comparison with experimental data from the Protein Data Bank, a correlation coefficient of 0.44 was found for chemical shift differences, and by accounting for uncertainty in experimental values, a correlation coefficient of 0.60 was obtained. ProCS is capable of identifying irregularly structured regions in proteins, such as the 66-120 segment of ubiquitin, and has been used to verify the structure of various proteins, including G-segment miniproteins with sequences derived from DNA barcode libraries. Additionally, ProCS has been found to be effective in refining protein structures by predicting chemical shifts for proteins with established three-dimensional folds, including ubiquitin and subdomains of larger proteins. This approach is expected to contribute significantly to the further development and validation of protein structure prediction, particularly for investigating distant regions in protein sequences. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the diverse range of losses available for different classification tasks. Despite widespread consensus on loss function best practices, a notable absence exists in literature regarding a comprehensive exploration of loss functions in deep learning applications. In this study, a broad selection of 77 loss functions was systematically evaluated across 112 datasets in 10 different domains to investigate their impact on model performance. Our investigation demonstrates that specific loss functions can yield superior results in particular datasets, underscoring the need to consider domain knowledge and data characteristics when making informed loss function choices. Furthermore, our analysis identifies areas for future research and reveals that certain loss functions remain underrepresented in the literature, while also highlighting the potential benefits of combining loss functions to improve model performance. Our open-source code is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/penm1234/Assessing-Loss-Functions. Comprehensive results are available online at https://www.penm1234.com/assessing-loss-functions. This work is an extension of the initial findings presented at MICAI 2021, which has been expanded to include experiments on 112 datasets in 10 different domains, from 4 new domains and 24 additional supervised regression tasks. Additionally, we rigorously test the robustness of the conclusions drawn through an extensive set of robustness assessments. These assessments have been conducted by multiple independent researchers who were asked to provide their views on the state-of-the-art loss functions for specific domains, based on their expertise. We propose a new framework called Minimax Engaged Learning (MEL) that dynamically changes its focus during training to maximize the discrepancy between a student model trying to replicate the teacher model's behavior, thereby pushing the teacher to higher levels of performance. MEL is a general model for both knowledge distillation and knowledge promotion, outperforming existing methods in various settings and achieving comparable results to current state-of-the-art supervised methods on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 benchmarks using ResNet-18 and ResNet-110 models. Notably, MEL reaches similar levels of accuracy as knowledge promotion methods but can also efficiently be applied to knowledge distillation tasks. Our study also shows that the effectiveness of MEL heavily depends on the chosen game strategy and the initialization of the teacher model, presenting a valuable area for further research in the future. The MEL framework has been implemented using PyTorch and is available for download at https://github.com/urchade/MEL.pytorch. To study the evolution of musical patterns, we analyze the information density in song lyrics and audio from the Billboard Top 100 charts spanning six decades. Measuring musical structure using entropy calculates the probability of occurring patterns within songs, yielding a complexity score that considers both the length and organization of those patterns. By comparing the time periods, we observe a decline in the complexity of song lyrics, inferred from the increased use of simpler sentence frameworks, and notice that the complexity of audio patterns is stable, yet became more fragmented over time. However, the more recent the period, the more frequently we notice deviations from expected musical patterns, revealed through the increasing prevalence of dissonance in songs. By correlating these findings with societal trends and artistic intentions, we make the case that the shift towards greater musical disorderliness is not a result of musicians making random changes, but rather the intentional adoption of a style characterized by contrast and variety. Moreover, our research finds no evidence that the changes in musical patterns are driven by factors such as genre, artist popularity, or song duration. Given the diverse range of songs used in our analysis, our results suggest that the influence of disorderly musical elements is a significant aspect of the style preferred by listeners in modern Western popular music. Ultimately, this research, centered around the application of complexity science to music, illuminates the significance of considering both the length and organization of patterns when evaluating complexity and reveals the existence of a distinction between the complexity of different musical representations. Additionally, it induces relevant readers to reflect on the evolution of the style in accordance with artistic principles. In a multiple-entry reinforcement process, distinct items are continuously added to a system and immediately assigned to active sequences based on a predetermined probability distribution assigned to the existing sequences. We examine the long-term dynamics of this process when the addition of new items occurs at an ever-increasing rate, analyzing both the sequence assignments and the underlying Markov process as the reinforcement rate approaches infinity. It is found that, under certain conditions, the system converges towards a stable state characterized by sequences of varying lengths following a specific distribution, known as the weak consistency property. Furthermore, we derive an explicit expression for the concentration function of the sequence length, representing the probability that the length of a random sequence falls within a specific interval. Additionally, we investigate the asymptotic length of sequences and its relationship to the specific characteristics of the underlying Markov process, establishing a general formula for the concentration function. These results are validated through numerical simulations, demonstrating excellent approximation when sampled at varying rates compared to theoretical predictions. Ludics is a mathematical framework for concurrent interaction developed by Girard, focusing on the core aspects of interaction and leaving aside the issues of linear logic's substrate. The key elements of Ludics are forking structures, representing the interactions of which the leaves denote the results. The choice of leaves is dictated by a notion of harmony, which serves as a central concept in the theory. This paper aims to provide an expanded interpretation of Ludics' core by introducing a semantics in a proof-based framework, leveraging the underlying topology of forking structures. We propose a semantics that incorporates harmonies as topological properties and demonstrate how this interpretation can be linked to the existing Curry-Howard analogy between proof and computation. This new semantics is closely related to the notion of witnessing in proof theory, which is commonly employed in proofs about functions, and it reveals a deeper connection between computational proof and Ludics-based interaction. We also show that this extended framework can be used to model dependent type theories by applying the Curry-Howard interpretation to dependent types, which is a novel approach. As a concrete example, we model the basic properties of the dependent type theory in Coq using Ludics-based interaction. This modeling not only provides a theoretical framework but also serves as a tool for understanding the computational essence of types and for leveraging the concepts of computational proof within a dependent type theory setting. By examining the notions of proof as a computational tool, we uncover various insights, such as the essential dependency between proof types and the proof-driven development of types, which is a key characteristic of Dependent Types. We also employ Ludics to define a concept for subtypes, which is dependent on the structure of dependent types, and we demonstrate how proof-driven development can be used to create a dependent type theory with encoded subtypes. Additionally, we model basic properties of Fregean Forcing, a concept introduced by Harper for understanding dependent types as a form of proof, using Ludics-based interaction. Forcing is a computational metaphor that views types as the result of propagating proof as computation through a pipe. By examining the dependency in proofs as in the case of Forcing, we gain insight into the dependency structure, which is a key aspect of understanding dependent types. We also show that by propagating proof as computation, it is possible to define dependent types in a proof-driven manner. A standard approach to modeling extreme events involves utilizing the distribution of exceedance times above certain threshold levels, often described through the use of a standard extreme-value process that incorporates a parameter linking threshold exceedance and time occurrences. However, this approach may result in Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) estimation difficulties due to the correlated nature of the extreme-value process, particularly when incorporating additional parameters that can affect estimation accuracy. To address these challenges, a study proposes a reparameterization method based on the Poisson process that separates the determination of threshold exceedance and time occurrence relationships, allowing for independent estimation of these key components of the extreme-value model. The study evaluates this method through simulations and extreme-value model estimation on synthetic data, demonstrating improved accuracy and performance. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the application of this method in modeling extreme weather events, utilizing data on daily maximum wind speed measurements from various locations in New Zealand's North Island. The results show that the reparameterization method enables the estimation of distinct parameters for different locations using a common set of data, reflecting the distinct climatic characteristics of those locations. The study also highlights the importance of considering spatial dependence in extreme-value model parameter estimation. The proposed method is subsequently compared to other approaches, showing its advantages in tackling complex estimation challenges and providing valuable insights into extreme-value model parameter behavior. The study's findings are consistent with previously observed trends in wind speed distributions. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research avenues, including the further development of the extreme-value model, particularly in considering the spatial relationships between locations. In Offline Reinforcement Learning, no explicit feedback is given to the learner through episodes that evolve over time.  Instead, a dataset of completed episodes is provided, allowing the agent to determine the best action given the observed state.  A key challenge in this area is solving the representation problem - selecting a representation that effectively captures state information to produce reliable policy outcomes.  This is complicated further by issues such as state-action masking and corruption, especially in complex domains.  In this research, we explore the impact of state-action corruption on representation learning, particularly in settings where the corruption is systematic and known to some degree.  This paper proposes a method to address corrupted data in RL, particularly in categories known as exploration vs. exploitation and multi-task reinforcement learning.  A key contribution of this paper is the development of a framework to create representations resilient to corruption, allowing for accurate policy recovery even with partially corrupted datasets in certain cases.  This research was facilitated through simulation using the AI2 School Shooting Dataset, a real-world dataset that exhibits corruptions in the state and action information.  This dataset is unique in its real-world context as it contains issues associated with corruptions commonly seen in real-life data but not typically found in standard reinforcement learning environments.  This research provides methods that effectively handle corrupted data, allowing for accurate policy recovery even with partially corrupted datasets in certain cases.  In particular, this research found that the development of resilient representations is dependent on several key factors including the level of corruption, the completeness of knowledge regarding corruption, and the underlying Markov Decision Process characteristics.  Specifically, this research demonstrated that it may be possible to recover accurate policies even with completely corrupted datasets in certain situations, such as when data is collected with an exploration policy.  This research does, however, acknowledge that representation learning with exploitation data alone can result in the recovery of inaccurate policies.  Additionally, this research found that it may be possible to recover accurate multi-task offline reinforcement learning policies even when multiple representations that effectively capture state information are partially corrupted.  This research utilized a concept known as information propagation, which suggests that a sufficiently long trajectory will contain enough information to effectively capture the state information in a representation. GJ 229B, discovered nearly two and a half decades ago, remains the first identified T-dwarf. Despite its notable discovery, the spectroscopic properties of GJ 229B, particularly in the mid-infrared region, have long been shrouded in uncertainty. Our analysis employed the APOLLO fast and accurate radiative transfer model, leveraging a comprehensive set of spectral databases, to constrain the atmospheric properties of GJ 229B using two broad bands from NICI and NIRC2 near-infrared spectra, as well as two Spitzer space telescope mid-infrared bands. Our model accounts for various atmospheric interactions including sphericity, temperature and pressure gradients, line broadening, particle scattering, absorption, emission, and phasing with the planet's rotation. By utilizing the EMEPAS chemical model, which accurately simulates atmospheric chemistry, we found that GJ 229B's atmosphere is composed of H2, H2O, CH4, NH3, and PH3. Our comprehensive analysis revealed the atmospheric characteristics of GJ 229B to be remarkably similar to those of 2MASS 0026, the second known T-dwarf object, particularly in terms of size, temperature, and composition. These similarities have further strengthened the notion of objects like GJ 229B and 2MASS 0026 serving as superior benchmarks for upcoming T-dwarf characterization campaigns. Our model predictions for the spectral properties of GJ 229B, particularly in the mid-infrared region, have addressed the uncertainty surrounding its discovery and have laid the groundwork for the utilization of the VLT-MACAO Grism Survey in the restriction of GJ 229B's chemical composition. The widespread availability of public transportation systems facilitates the movement of a great many people in urban areas, necessitating a consideration of how airborne pathogens can be transmitted on public transportation and in other crowded settings. To better understand these dynamics and evaluate the effectiveness of different intervention strategies, researchers have developed mathematical models describing the flow of individuals through these environments. Notably, a simple model has been proposed for urban buses, which assumes a limitless supply of passengers waiting to board, following the principles of a well-mixed system. This model assumes that air currents distribute viruses uniformly throughout the vehicle's air space, facilitating transmission between passengers. Notably, the model has predicted a high transmission rate under crowded conditions and no transmission under less crowded conditions when wearing masks. In the present study, we validated the predictions of this mathematical model through comparison with computational simulations that modeled an actual urban bus environment. Specifically, we used particle modeling to track the movement of air particles and viruses in a simulated bus environment, representing a bus trip with 120 passengers and an occupancy rate of 80% or higher. In particular, we varied the duration of the trip, the number of tripping cycles, and the initial concentration of viruses. Our results indicated a high correlation between the model's predictions and the results of the computational simulations, with an average error of less than 0.7%. In general, the model tended to slightly underestimate the transmission rate, particularly when the duration of the trip was less than the time it took for air currents to circulate throughout the vehicle. Discussion of these findings is presented in the attached file. In essence, this validation supports the use of the mathematical model as a useful tool for evaluating the effectiveness of different intervention strategies on urban buses, such as the distribution of masks to all passengers or the sanitizing of bus air systems. Additionally, this model can be expanded to predict transmission in other crowded settings, such as movie theaters, concert halls, and other crowded settings. Furthermore, we recognized the limitations of our model, which did not take into account the actual movement of individuals through these environments or the distribution of viruses on surfaces that can transmit the virus. Nonetheless, our model provides a useful starting point for evaluating the effectiveness of different intervention strategies in these high-risk settings. In conclusion, this research can contribute to informing policies aimed at mitigating the spread of airborne pathogens in urban areas, particularly through public transportation systems. In essence, our research can help to identify the most effective intervention strategies, such as the distribution of masks to all passengers or the sanitizing of bus air

Despite its advantages, the standard DMD method exhibits limitations when applied to non-linear systems, and its performance is also susceptible to disruptions from minor noise levels. In an effort to overcome these challenges, a novel data-driven framework called Linear and Nonlinear Clarification Optimization (LANDO) has been formulated to improve DMD, particularly in non-linear systems and those affected by noise. This framework involves reformulating the non-linear system into an equivalent effective linear system, and it can be applied to identify the structure of complex systems under various conditions. In this study, the effectiveness of LANDO was demonstrated in several numerical and real-world scenarios, and it was shown to enhance the accuracy of DMD when dealing with non-linear systems, and also to facilitate the discovery of hidden system dynamics when the input data is incomplete. The analysis indicates that AIC leads to a shorter spin period, increased spin velocity, and higher magnetic field strength for MSPs. Furthermore, we established a novel correlation between the MSP spin period (or velocity) and its magnetic field strength, and also discovered a relationship between these parameters and the mass accretion rate in the moments preceding the AIC. The findings suggest that the pale dwarf MSP population differs significantly from that observed in the galactic disk, primarily due to varying star formation rates and different late-time X-ray binary evolution pathways.
