Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we develop a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the mass and angular momentum of extreme black holes following specific perturbations. The Iyer-Wald formalism yields the most stringent bound on these corrections, suggesting that they are composed solely of non-negative quantities. Building upon this method, we develop a systematic approach for obtaining precise algebraic expressions governing these corrections, specifically for the Schwarzschild, Reissner-Nordstrom, and de Sitter black holes in four dimensions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Iyer-Wald formalism can be adapted to probe corrections in non-extreme black holes as well. The key challenge in obtaining these corrections revolves around identifying an appropriate perturbation vector field that satisfies the necessary conditions stipulated by the Iyer-Wald formalism. In this context, our work involves developing a set of heuristic rules that can aid in identifying such a perturbation vector field in various black hole spacetimes. Ultimately, our findings reveal that the nature of the corrections depends on the specific characteristics of the black hole spacetimes, leading to distinct correction patterns in their mass and angular momentum profiles. Specifically, for the Schwarzschild and Reissner-Nordstrom spacetimes, we demonstrate that the mass and angular momentum corrections exhibit similar patterns, whereas the de Sitter spacetime yields distinct correction profiles. Moreover, our work serves as a testament to the effectiveness of the Iyer-Wald formalism in obtaining rigorous bounds on these corrections. Additionally, our findings underscore the significance of developing a deeper understanding of the gauge invariance inherent in classical general relativity, particularly in its implications for the Iyer-Wald formalism. Lastly, we propose that our method can be adapted and applied to various other black hole spacetimes, thereby expanding the scope of the Iyer-Wald formalism in obtaining corrections for a wide array of black hole solutions. Specifically, we envision that our approach can be applied to probe corrections in the Kerr metric, as well as more complex spacetimes such as the black holes with nonlinear electrodynamics and cosmological constant. In this regard, our work serves as a foundational framework for a more comprehensive strategy that can utilize the Iyer-Wald formalism to explore the intricate world of classical black hole corrections. Ultimately, by adapting and refining our method, we aim to unravel the intricate nature of classical general relativity, particularly in its applications to black hole physics. Additionally, our work may hold the potential for significant cross-disciplinary implications, thereby expanding our current understanding of spacetime

A key aspect of effective motor learning is how the body plans and executes movements, with significant benefits arising from the interplay between these processes in terms of learning efficiency. To delve deeper into the purpose behind this productive cycle of movement generation and learning, a method is developed to identify areas of high value within the state space of movements. This high-value area is where the most effective learning occurs, enabling improvements in movement performance through the self-correcting process. By effectively learning from mistakes, the system becomes more adept at producing the desired outcomes. As a result, productively active movements, such as those engaged in by self-healing systems like humans, can be distinguished from the randomly active movements of robots like the blind search algorithm, which provide a valuable comparison for understanding motor learning mechanisms. To test the proposed end-effect evaluation strategy, a basic motor learning algorithm is created using simple 2D trajectories and applied to a 2DoF robot arm under various initial condition scenarios. The approach shows promise in identifying high-value areas for productive movement and could be adapted for use in more complex systems. Furthermore, the high potential for improvement in robotic arm control using this end-effect evaluation strategy suggests its relevance and potential impact on the development of robotic motor skills. We examine the problem of creating a straight-line planar drawing when each node is connected to at least one edge. This can be viewed as an application of the H-Substructure Problem, a concept introduced by Fiala and Giannopoulou. By leveraging parameterized approaches, we develop efficient algorithms to solve this problem in cases where the number of components in the input graph is constrained. Specifically, we provide a fixed-parameter algorithm based on tractable separators and an alternative method using partitioning schemes to restrict the size of sub-graphs considered during the drawing construction process. Both of these algorithms yield desirable results when combined with parameterized deletion schemes that can remove edges from the graph. This leads to a $O(3.25^k n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$) time complexity for solving the H-Substructure Problem when k edges are deleted. We also explore the application of parameterized deletion schemes to the Upward Planarity problem when edges are removed to improve the algorithm's efficiency when dealing with constrained parameter values. This leads to an $O(1.854^k n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$) time complexity for solving the Upward Planarity problem with k edges deleted. Both of these parameterized algorithms are novel contributions and have not been previously published. Finally, we examine the related problem of Constrained Upward Planarity, which involves creating a straight-line drawing where nodes connected by more than one edge are at least $\epsilon$ distance apart. This problem can be viewed as an application of the H-Substructure Problem with additional constraints. We provide a fixed-parameter algorithm based on $\epsilon$-spider decompositions to solve this problem efficiently when the number of components in the input graph is constrained, leading to an $O(2.0625^k n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$) time complexity for solving the Constrained Upward Planarity problem with k components. This approach combined with a new $\epsilon$-spider deletion scheme yields an $O(1.90625^k n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$) time complexity for solving the Constrained Upward Planarity problem with k edges deleted. This research presents several new parameterized algorithms for creating a straight-line planar drawings in cases where the number of components in the input graph is constrained. This includes efficient algorithm for solving Upward Planarity and Constrained Upward Planarity problems using parameterized deletion schemes that remove edges from the graph.

This paper explores the capabilities of finite-state channels with feedback, assuming the receiver has complete knowledge of the transmission channel. We demonstrate that this scenario enables error-free information transmission over any finite-state channel, which is equivalent to achieving perfect error correction in a finite number of steps, known as finite memory. Specifically, we show that a reliable encoder can utilize past and future data to create a sequence that is perfectly decodable by a variable-rate decoder, working within a finite memory scope. Building upon this insight, we prove that there exists an encoder/decoder pair achieving near-capacity performance, utilizing sequential transmission and feedback, for any target error rate and finite memory constraints. Furthermore, we establish that the optimal decoding strategy for this scenario is equivalent to solving a min-max problem in the space of finite-state machines, which models the worst-case channel distortions. We also provide a concise description of the optimal decoding algorithm, known as the sequential decoding with feedback (SDF) algorithm, along with an analysis of its computational complexity. Notably, in cases where the channel transition probabilities are stationary and ergodic, the computational complexity of SDF is shown to be sub-exponential. We also propose a heuristic approximation to SDF, which is computationally efficient and achieves notable performance improvements in scenarios with short memory constraints. These findings are substantiated through numerical simulations. Ultimately, this research contributes to our understanding of feedback in finite-state channels, providing valuable insights for practical implementations. We exemplify this research's relevance by applying the developed algorithms to solve a real-world problem, accurately decoding a sequence of symbols transmitted over a real-world channel with feedback. The proposed algorithms are made available through an open-source software package on GitHub. It is noteworthy that this research was initially published under the title "Feedback in Finite-State Channels," in the 2022 IEEE Information Theory Workshop. This document differs from the original publication by incorporating additional insights and developments. In particular, this document presents a novel approach to approximating the optimal decoding algorithm, which is distinct from the publication's content. This work has investigated the potential of integrating an ozone O3 and ultraviolet (UV) light system for effectively eliminating sulfur dioxide (SO2) emissions in flue gas. So far, UV light treatment alone has been primarily utilized to oxidize SO2, yet the system's overall efficiency heavily relies on the UV lamp's power consumption. In contrast, an O3-based system has been shown to achieve higher removal rates, yet the generated O3 is largely used to absorb SO2, leading to unnecessary energy expenditure. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the effect of O3 addition on the energy efficiency of the UV/O3 system in removing SO2. It was found that the energy efficiency of the combined UV/O3 system increased by 30% compared to the standalone UV light treatment. Furthermore, a mathematical model was developed to quantify the contribution of O3 to the removal of SO2, revealing that a 100 ppm O3 concentration could enhance the energy efficiency by 26.5% or increase the total removal rate by 12% when no O3 was present. Based on these findings, the study suggests integrating an O3 generator with the existing UV light technology to boost the energy efficiency of SO2 removal in flue gas treatment. Additionally, an O3 concentration above 150 ppm was required to optimize the energy efficiency of the integrated system, with higher concentrations showing diminishing returns. Notably, the study observed an 95% removal rate for SO2 emissions in the flue gas treatment process, achieving excellent results and providing valuable insights for implementing the ozone/UV system in practice. It is expected that further optimizations and advancements could yield even more compelling outcomes. Lastly, the study confirmed that no by-products or pollutants were emitted during the ozone/UV treatment process, aligning with previous research on the topic. In conclusion, the integrated ozone/UV system represented a viable and effective solution for eliminating sulfur dioxide emissions in flue gas, offering improved energy efficiency and high removal rates with minimal energy input. With potential applications extending beyond air pollution to the development of novel materials and industrial processes, the ozone/UV technology provided a promising approach for tackling various environmental and chemical challenges. To further refine the ozone/UV system, the study recommended conducting more in-depth examinations of the treatment process, including kinetic analysis and assessments of system scalability and cost. It is anticipated that these efforts will yield significant outcomes in the fields of environmental science and chemical engineering. Machine learning algorithms can be quite effective, but they often rely on data that's poorly defined, leading to model inconsistencies and unreliable outcomes. This study introduces a novel machine learning framework, Indecision Forests, which enables learning to classify data under uncertain premises. Inspired by classical logic and possible world semantics, Indecision Forests represents knowledge as a network of connected facts and rules, allowing for the calculation of a probability distribution based on possible world semantics. This approach can be scaled up for large datasets using approximate inference methods. Experiments have demonstrated the benefits of Indecision Forests in handling uncertain data, even when traditional machine learning algorithms struggle with poorly defined data. Additionally, a model pre-trained on general knowledge can be adapted to solve specific tasks by incorporating domain-specific information. Although direct application of Indecision Forests to new tasks is computationally challenging, research has shown the potential for knowledge transfer and domain adaptation. This has far-reaching implications for various industries, including the legal system, where argumentation-based reasoning with quantified uncertainty is particularly relevant. The source code for Indecision Forests is available on GitHub at https://github.com/mdotley/indecision_forests. A demonstration is available at https://indecision.universite-paris-saclay.fr. This research is based on prior work cited within the paper and has been publicly presented at NeurIPS 2019 under the same title.

Current educational approaches in testing receive minimal attention, with professors typically relying on thorough feedback from students to identify areas of improvement. However, this approach can be inefficient, demanding a substantial amount of time from instructors. To address this, we present a testing framework that utilizes inquiry-based testing as a way to provide conceptual feedback to students, saving instructors time and enabling them to focus on guiding students through testing principles. We compared the effectiveness of this conceptual feedback method with the traditional thorough feedback method through a study involving 244 undergraduate students in two different semesters. The results showed that conceptual feedback reduced the time spent by instructors on providing feedback by 70%, with no statistically significant differences in test coverage rates between the two methods. We discuss the implications of this finding and highlight its potential to improve teaching efficiency in software testing education. Furthermore, we highlight the limitations of our study and suggest potential areas for further research. We believe that this research will facilitate the development of more efficient educational testing approaches, enhancing the overall quality of software testing education. The testing framework used in this research is freely available at https://github.com/TestProcessTestingInstructor/TestProjectForInstructor. We are open to collaborating on further research; please feel free to contact us at your convenience.

Researchers have extensively explored Graph Convolutional Networks, a powerful neural network design for node classification in graph-based data. Despite the significant advancements, there's a notable limitation: GCNs effectively ignore the global structure of the graph, only incorporating local information. This seems to be an inherent characteristic of the Graph Convolutional Networks architecture. In this study, we introduce a novel perspective on GCNs, revealing that their convolutional components act as 'over-blurring' agents, diminishing the global graph features. This understanding allows us to develop a simple yet effective improvement, EnhanceGN, which leverages the global structure by preserving the graph's initial features. By doing so, we achieve state-of-the-art performance on six publicly available benchmark datasets. Moreover, we show that EnhanceGN's success is not simply a by-product of increased model capacity, as supported by the analysis of its Generalization Error Gap. Finally, we test GCNs across 34 public datasets and find that EnhanceGN consistently outperforms the best existing method in approximately 61% of these benchmarks. The source code is available at https://github.com/ericoyarasa/EnhanceGN.

We propose new kernel-dependent distribution functions for quasi-particles that depend on $k_\perp$ depending on the degree of particle fragmentation, enabling a thorough examination of particle fragmentation effects in Heavy Ion Collisions. These functions are contrasted with conventional distribution functions, including those developed by Strickland and Greco, in various fragmentation scenarios. Furthermore, we show that our approach can be applied to both ab initio calculations and Effective Kinetic Theory treatments, such as those based on KLN theory and the $T$-matrix kinetic theory. These novel functions are then utilised to compute the mean multiplicity of charged particles as a function of transverse momentum in Pb-Pb collisions at LHC's highest energy. Our findings indicate that particle fragmentation significantly influences the measurement, resulting in a higher multiplicity at higher transverse momentum than would be predicted by kinematic considerations alone. Importantly, the difference between our proposed functions and the conventional distribution functions serves as a quantitative indicator of particle fragmentation effects. We anticipate that this work will serve as a fundamental foundation for the analysis of particle fragmentation effects in Heavy Ion Collisions at the LHC's highest energy. Additionally, we suggest an analogous approach for baryon-holding particles, incorporating features of DiQuark Higgsification, with a view to reinterpreting long-standing anomalies in Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. These novel distribution functions can be accessed through our public website. This concept can be further developed through categorifying the mapping between these functionals and states. By treating linear functionals as coefficients, any quantum operation can be represented as a linear map between specific bimodules. This framework: establishes that linear functionals, defined on a particular algebra, can be viewed as sections of a 2-categorical bundle; demonstrates that linear maps between these functionals are equivalent to morphisms between the underlying bimodules; shows that the composition of linear functionals corresponds to the tensor product of bimodules; and, in Gelfand duality-equivalent cases, generalizes the C*-algebraic GNS-construction, linking von Neumann algebras, GNS bimodules, and cyclic states. These include a broad range of dualities, multiple forms of equivalence between theories, and the deep connection between abstract duality theory and the established results. Finally, this work presents a new approach to constructing covariant duality theories for abstract quantum theories, enabling the generalization of duality theory to categories of quantum theories that do not have a dual category. This paper extends our previous work by removing the minimal boundary assumption and considering more general boundaries resulting from partial compactifications of the foliation. A key component of our study involves the development of an invariant called 'essence' to gauge the distortion of measured foliations, which enables us to prove that small changes in the foliation's boundary lead to small changes in the associated measured foliation. This research also has implications for understanding the differential of the mapping sending boundaries to measured foliations, which is currently under investigation. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and listening to heart sounds has long been a key part of this process for healthcare professionals. However, machine-based approaches have been hampered by the challenging acquisition of high-quality audio data, especially when dealing with noisy environments and the inherent distortions inherent in the recording process. To address this, this study focuses on developing effective methods for categorizing heart sounds that take into account these environmental and recording limitations. Two new approaches were explored and compared to established techniques: a robust optimization method and a multi-scale, deep learning-based fusion algorithm utilizing wavelet transforms. When evaluated on a particular dataset, the wavelet-based method emerged as the top performer, surpassing other techniques by a significant margin in accuracy while also remaining adaptable to various environmental noise levels. The study's findings demonstrate the importance of considering the specific data capture context in designing heart sound classification systems. With continued advancements in recording technology, deep learning models like this one may become even more practical tools for healthcare use. This research focuses on investigating twisted bounded domains in the plane, specifically those with a symmetry twist, by examining their properties when enclosed by a unit torus. The study considers all possible 2D crystallographic point groups and their associated domain twisting phenomena. The main aim is to establish the relationship between the group order and the number of distinct twisted domains, as well as to determine the conditions under which these domains can be found within the torus interior. The results show that the number of these twisted domains is directly related to the order of the group and can be calculated using the twisted fundamental group. The study further advances the concept of domain twisting by demonstrating that multiple domain twisting is feasible if the group action involves a torsion greater than 2. Additionally, the research delves into characterizing the twisted domains when the group action corresponds to a torsion of 2, which involves using topological invariants from K-theory to establish the classification system. The study includes examples and illustrations to complement the theoretical findings and outlines potential future research directions in this area. The associated data, including group action tables, group orders, and numerical results, is available for download on a dedicated repository. The research hopes to stimulate further exploration into the geometric and topological properties of domain twisting in scenarios with crystalline symmetry. The study also highlights potential links to existing theories in topological quantum mechanics and condensed matter physics. Finally, the research encourages future research into the diversity of domain twisting phenomena through the application of modern algebraic techniques to the study of domain twisting in crystals. Human societies that closely collaborate for mutual benefits tend to thrive better, especially in the long run. This resilient capacity is closely linked to our ability to work together to address global threats like climate change. To better understand and make informed decisions about climate policy, it's essential to develop effective communication strategies that leverage community strengths, fostering cooperative action in the face of global challenges despite our differences. Building on established knowledge about human communication patterns, social connections, and environmental concerns, this article explores how community dynamics can be harnessed to address climate change through collaborative efforts. It examines the essential elements of successful climate communication, including local-level initiatives that emphasize shared goals, collective action, and the positive impact of cooperative efforts on our well-being, as well as the critical need to address social inequities that undermine fair climate change discussions and policies in vulnerable communities. Finally, it highlights key challenges and opportunities for developing climate change communication strategies that foster cooperative action, promote just transitions, and support fair distribution of resources in vulnerable communities, while also promoting individual agency and choice in addressing global problems.

We investigate the feasibility of creating paintings using only GANs, relying on nothing more than the input of a color. This innovative approach is inspired by the artistic movement of Abstract Expressionism, which sought to capture the inner spirit of a person through art. By leveraging a generator network, we demonstrate that paintings can be generated, and then utilize a discriminator network to refine the output. Additionally, we break down the painting process into component parts, such as edges and textures, to explore their respective roles. This breakdown enables multiple parallel generators to collaborate on creating a painting, each focusing on a specific element, resulting in a more detailed and visually appealing outcome. Our research culminates in a demonstration video showcasing the step-by-step painting process, from edges to a completed picture. This unprecedented method achieves remarkable results, producing high-resolution 512x512 resolution paintings in just 30-40 steps, equivalent to a timeline of 2-3 seconds. Most remarkably, each generated painting is accompanied by an exact metering of color metrics, ensuring consistency with the input color provided by the artist. This research opens doors to new and exciting areas of exploration, including the generation of paintings tailored to specific styles and genres, facilitated by the Delight Neural Paintings framework. Academic researchers often rely on Google to find relevant information and answer their questions, but a significant portion of Google searches are driven by academic inquiries. We have collected a dataset of over 12,000 questions from scientific researchers, along with answers provided by Google's Knowledge Graph feature, which is linked to research papers on Semantic Scholar. We have developed an approach that uses natural language processing and information retrieval techniques to recommend relevant research papers in response to these questions. We have evaluated our method in a user study that involved 219 researchers, demonstrating improved outcomes in terms of relevance and satisfaction compared to a baseline approach that simply recommends recently published papers. Our dataset and open-source code are available for others to build upon our findings. Ultimately, we aim to enhance the ability of researchers to find answers to their questions by providing more targeted recommendations of relevant research papers. We believe this goal aligns with the values of the Semantic Scholar community, which is to empower researchers to get the most out of academic research by making it easily discoverable and accessible. We envision several potential applications derived from this research, including integrating our question-answering capability into research papers, enabling search within research papers, and providing recommendations based on questions in research papers. Additionally, we believe our dataset could be useful in training question-answering models, a task that is essential for natural language processing and has significant practical implications. In the event of core collapse, a massive star transforms into a supernova, and neutrinos, heavily interacted with the star's matter due to their significant mass difference, escape from the star's core. This leads to neutrino oscillations and may result in neutrino flavor instability developing in the region where neutrinos are born. Studying this phenomenon in three-dimensional supernova models, researchers analyzed the instability's growth rate and velocity in various supernova scenarios. They discovered that the instability's growth rate is primarily determined by how far neutrinos travel within the star's core and the angle-dependent velocity of the instability's initial perturbations. In a newly formed black hole supernova model, neutrino flavor instability may develop into a persistent, spiral-like structure due to the complex, twisting velocity pattern caused by the star's initial spin. This structure may persist for several tens of milliseconds and could potentially influence the late stages of supernova development. However, in models representing non-rotating stars, the instability's structure is less complex, and it may disappear within tens to hundreds of milliseconds. Nevertheless, in all models examined, the instability leads to mass transport of neutrinos by millions of grams per second at peak instability levels, which could impact supernova development and neutrino fluxes observed from Earth. Researchers therefore recommend incorporating this phenomenon into models of supernova development to gain a more comprehensive understanding of core-collapse events. Additionally, future multi-dimensional simulations in greater detail are required to expand upon these preliminary findings. Specifically, rough estimates suggest that any flavor-dependent neutrino opacities could amplify the instability's growth rate by a factor of two. Various factors may therefore ultimately affect the final stages and observed characteristics of supernovae. Ultimately, neutrino flavor instability may lead to more robust and dynamic supernova development. If this phenomenon leads to observable changes in supernova light, it may provide valuable insight into heavy elements within nearby stars. If neutrino flavor instability triggers a collapse of the stellar core, it could result in the birth of a heavy neutron star. In the case of complete core collapse, this phenomenon may provide insight into heavy neutron star properties. Lastly, neutrino flavor instability may lead to distinct neutrino signals observed from nearby stars and could potentially influence our understanding of the supernova related to SN1987A. In summary, incorporating neutrino flavor instability into supernova models may yield numerous and diverse consequences for supernova development, neutron star properties, and the detection of core-collapse events. ADHD is a widely prevalent psychiatric condition that has been challenging to diagnose accurately. Recent advancements in machine learning have the potential to improve diagnostic processes, specifically with data-driven approaches using resting-state fMRI brain images and deep learning models. However, the success of these models heavily relies on properly identifying and incorporating essential brain regions for the task at hand. In the case of ADHD diagnosis, there is a notable shortage of research examining which brain regions are crucial for delivering accurate diagnoses. In our study, we conducted comprehensive evaluations to pinpoint the essential components of the brain for ADHD diagnosis and investigated the impact of using various preservation techniques on a deep learning model's performance. Notably, our findings suggest that a sparse average technique outperformed other methods, and when employed in a state-of-the-art deep learning model, resulted in superior performance compared to previous studies using rs-fMRI data. Ultimately, our work contributes to the development of more accurate ADHD diagnoses through the identification of critical brain regions for the task and informs future research with insights on utilizing preservation techniques to improve deep learning models. Additionally, our code is publicly available for reproduction of our results and future applications. We found that a model trained on rs-fMRI data from 198 subjects (including 84 ADHD patients) could achieve high accuracy in ADHD diagnosis by leveraging a small subset of 62 critical brain regions, and that certain models trained on rs-fMRI data from individuals with the ADHD label only could achieve even higher accuracy in ADHD diagnosis by utilizing a smaller number of brain regions compared to models trained on data with opposing labels. Furthermore, our research involved evaluations of common problems such as class imbalance and identified that data augmentation did not notably impact the performance of the model. In contrast, our findings suggest that utilizing techniques for balancing data had a more considerable impact on the model's performance compared to data augmentation. Additionally, we conducted a series of ablation studies to examine the performance of the model when trained on progressively smaller datasets and found that the model's performance in ADHD diagnosis declines as the size of the training dataset decreases. Nonetheless, our research involved simulations to explore the model's potential for generalizing to larger datasets and yielded promising results. In summary, our research contributes to the development of more accurate ADHD diagnoses through ADHD-fMRI data analysis and identifies critical brain regions for the task, as well as the most effective preservation techniques for this particular diagnostic task. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly when used in lengthy texts or across different contexts. To address the challenges posed by acronyms, effective detection and disambiguation strategies are essential to enhance text processing quality. In response to the growing acronym-related data risks, researchers are beginning to acknowledge the importance of accurate acronym detection and disambiguation in natural language processing tasks. To contribute to ongoing efforts and standardize evaluation procedures, this paper presents MadDog, a comprehensive web-based platform for acronym identification and disambiguation. The platform offers a range of features that enable researchers to access and utilize previously collected data, conduct their own annotations, and securely upload and share annotated datasets. Additionally, MadDog facilitates the standardization of evaluation procedures, allowing researchers to replicate and compare previous results and gain insight into the performance of their own models on established datasets. We highlight the technical aspects and infrastructure that enabled the development of MadDog, as well as its annotated datasets, which amount to 14,779 sentences spanning 5,921 unique acronyms across three domains. Our analysis demonstrates that MadDog's standard evaluation procedures match the specifications proposed by the NAIDAC benchmark, solidifying its status as a versatile and adaptable solution for acronym identification and disambiguation. We believe that MadDog will serve as a valuable resource for the natural language processing community, catering to the needs of researchers working on related challenges. We expect its features and infrastructure to be utilized in various data annotation and understanding tasks, extending beyond the acronym domain. Quantum interference, evident in low-dimensional systems, is one of the most notable manifestations of quantum physics. Historically, quantum interference has been observed in charge transport; however, recent findings indicate that it also plays a crucial role in thermoelectric effects and heat transfer. We investigate the interplay between quantum interference and heat transfer within complex nanostructures, beginning with a fundamental examination of heat transfer between two dissimilar materials and followed by a detailed analysis of a quantum Hall junction featuring edge channels, where interference arises from various interference loops of different chiralities. Due to interference, the thermoelectric current and heat transfer between channels exhibit reversible switching in response to external stimuli, in addition to displaying directional heat transfer. By manipulating inter-connectors and edge-bends within the Hall junction, we showcase the potential to develop multi-functional nano-devices that simultaneously generate heat, rectify heat, convert mechanical to electrical energy, and store electrical energy. Consequently, these devices can be used in the development of compact, self-cooling devices, as well as artificial nano-machines where internal heat generation is a concern. Ultimately, these novel nano-devices offer a means to manipulate charge, heat, and magnetic properties at exceptionally low temperatures. For example, two devices that rectify heat and convert mechanical to electrical energy operate optimally at temperatures of 0.5K and 1K, respectively. We hope that these findings will stimulate the development of innovative, multi-functional nano-devices that exploit quantum interference for practical purposes. A cutting-edge technology for data storage, based on DNA molecules, has shown significant long-term potential due to its exceptionally low cost per bit and incredibly long data retention period. Although recent advancements have made DNA data extraction more efficient, the process of creating ordered DNA sequences to represent hierarchical data structures still presents significant challenges. To address these issues, a novel approach called $\textsf{DNAstr}$ is introduced, providing a comprehensive system that effectively supports hierarchical data structures and efficient data updates while taking advantage of recent breakthroughs in DNA sequence construction. The $\textsf{DNAstr}$ system incorporates several innovative features, including a top-down construction method for hierarchical sequences, a novel data encoding technique using straight-line paths, and a dynamic fixed-point computation framework to facilitate efficient data updates. The performance of $\textsf{DNAstr}$ is evaluated through both theoretical analysis and experimental validation, demonstrating superior performance in update operations, sequence retrieval, and data construction, when compared to existing DNA data storage methods. The results show that $\textsf{DNAstr}$ can achieve a significant improvement of up to $38\%$ in update efficiency and provide faster sequence retrieval at a rate of up to $6.8\%$ higher than the best current method. The $\textsf{DNAstr}$ evaluation confirmed that this innovative approach outperforms cutting-edge DNA data storage solutions in both theoretical analysis and practical experiments. The work on $\textsf{DNAstr}$ represents an important advancement in the development of efficient DNA data storage methods to support complex hierarchical data structures and efficient data updates. The project website with all the source code, experimental data, and detailed documentation is available at: \url{https://dnastr.cs.uic.edu/}. The $\textsf{DNAstr}$ team is committed to continuously developing and improving this innovative approach, and it welcomes feedback, questions, and suggestions from the community. In oscillatory media, regions that oscillate faster than their surroundings can act as pacemakers, generating waves through their movement. This is the underlying mechanism behind numerous biological phenomena, such as muscle contraction and neuronal signaling. By applying an approximation method, we have developed and compared three formulas for calculating the speed of these waves in two different types of oscillatory media. Our analysis reveals that two of these formulas are equally accurate and can be used in both linear and nonlinear systems, while a third formula is suitable for specific nonlinear cases. Furthermore, we have shown that these formulas can be applied not only in one-dimensional systems but also in dimensions one order higher. We validate our findings by testing them in a model based on the intrinsic property of cardiac myocytes. Our work expects to contribute to a deeper understanding of wave propagation in oscillatory media. Additionally, these estimations may facilitate the development of mathematical and computational models in biological and chemical contexts. We believe that these formulas can be adapted for exploring wave phenomena in other dimensions, including higher dimensions beyond the three-dimensional world. Lastly, we hope that our research will stimulate further investigation into the theoretical aspects of pacemaker-generated waves. We have made public all of the codes related to this research, allowing other scientists to build upon our findings. We invite colleagues to join us in further exploring the topics mentioned above. We have developed two distinct algorithms for approximating the von Neumann entropy (NE) of a quantum state, one for classical-quantum and fully quantum systems. The first algorithm works by randomly sampling purified states and using the relative entropy to estimate NE, while the second employs a modified version of a sampling approach initially proposed in arXiv:1806.027er. Both algorithms are found to converge at a sublinear rate at the population level, offering an improvement over previous methods at the zeroth population level. Additionally, we have verified that these algorithms can achieve convergence rates orders of magnitude faster when utilized in conjunction with infra-red transformations. The empirical analysis demonstrates that the NE estimation algorithms perform significantly better, especially for low-purification levels, either standalone or when employed with the aforementioned transformations. Furthermore, we have observed that the modified sampling approach can be successfully applied across a wide range of non-convergence scenarios. The empirical results suggest that NE can be accurately estimated at a relatively low computational cost when NE is predominantly determined by short-range interactions in the quantum circuit architecture. The output of this research can contribute to the development of more resource-efficient quantum algorithms for approximating NE. The source code associated with this research is publicly accessible via https://github.com/yashar-irani/NE-estimation. New types of quantum processors are emerging, which utilize quantum algorithms to equip classical machines with analytical capabilities. Yet, current understanding of these algorithms is largely theoretical, and their efficacy is difficult to assess. We explore the potential of utilizing quantum algorithms for unsupervised learning tasks and discover that existing instructional data can be leveraged to generate multiple states, which in turn enables the extraction of valuable information. We find that variations within the instructional data yield distinct states, whereas differences between instructional sets result in overlapping distributions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a variation of the quantum algorithm can induce state collapse upon encountering divergent data, effectively selecting a specific state. Our findings indicate that quantum algorithms can be applied beyond traditional supervised learning paradigms and hold promise for a range of unsupervised and guided learning applications. We propose the term multi-modal quantum learning to describe this capability, in which instructional data from different modes gives rise to distinct states, enabling tasks such as joint processing of data from multiple sources or selecting a specific state when presented with ambiguous information. We illustrate the potential of multi-modal quantum learning by showing that the instructional data associated with readout measurements and control tones can be utilized to extract features in audio signals. This approach to multi-modal quantum learning demonstrates the promise of harnessing quantum algorithms to equip machines with analytical capabilities across diverse data types and domains. We describe an experimental protocol for observing quantum algorithm-induced state manipulation, either through variations within instructional data or multi-modal approaches, which could serve as a benchmark for evaluating the performance of quantum processors. We propose a novel application of quantum algorithms in guided learning, which involves using the instructional data to select a specific state when presented with ambiguous information, and demonstrate its potential in paired learning, where two quantum processors exchange information to enhance the performance of existing algorithms. Our study offers a comprehensive understanding of the capabilities and potential applications of quantum algorithms across a range of unsupervised and guided learning paradigms. We propose a new, iterative method for accurately calculating shadowing between complex objects, enabling its use in differentiable optimization frameworks for inverse problems such as image synthesis and 3D shape recovery. Traditional shadowing algorithms rely on simplified approaches that are not suitable for differentiable optimization, so we adapt a widely employed ray-tracing algorithm to a novel optimization framework. By formulating shadowing as a resolution of a ray-tracing equation, we develop an iterative method that incorporates sign-function approximations and Newton's method for efficient convergence. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in synthesizing images and recovering 3D shapes under varying lighting conditions, outperforming a comparison method based on approximate shadowing algorithms. Additionally, we showcase its integration in a differentiable optimization framework for image synthesis. This methodical approach allows researchers to gather more accurate information and reduce the reliance on intuition or bias when selecting hyperparameters for future investigation. Ultimately, this approach can aid researchers in prioritizing which hyperparameters to modify or investigate further.

Reinforcement learning has achieved significant success in various domains. Nevertheless, a major area of limited exploration remains - online learning in dynamic environments. In such settings, cumulative knowledge from past experiences is applied to improve future outcomes in an ever-changing landscape. In the realm of medical research, this concept is particularly pertinent, with online learning expected to transform clinical practice and public health by utilizing real-time data. Unfortunately, a notable absence of standardized evaluation frameworks hinders the comparison and advancement of online learning methods. In an effort to fill this gap, we present L2Explorer, a groundbreaking framework that simulates real-world online learning scenarios with adjustable dynamics. L2Explorer encompasses a suite of 12 diverse evaluation scenarios, encompassing both synthetic and true-to-life data, as well as a comprehensive set of performance metrics. L2Explorer is built with scalability in mind, allowing for the effortless integration of new evaluation scenarios and a range of 12 already implemented. These evaluation scenarios cover critical areas such as disease prevention, treatment, and risk assessment, as well as a broad spectrum of learning dynamics, including stochastic, bias-driven, and adversarial processes. Furthermore, we have developed a range of baseline models targeting different aspects of online learning, as well as a comprehensive study demonstrating the distinct strengths and limitations of these models in comparison to the best-known approaches in the field. L2Explorer is now freely available, with the aim of accelerating research in online learning and shaping the future of lifelong reinforcement learning. A comprehensive repository containing all the source code and evaluation scenarios can be accessed via https://github.com/ImpactScience/L2Explorer. A public dashboard showcasing the results of our research can be found at https://l2explorer.io. A detailed report on our research is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.07133. In addition, the data used in our research is openly available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9f90.v1.0. Firstly, by formulating an optimization problem that minimizes the difference between measured data and responses simulated under the 'outside in' scenario, the boundary can be accurately located. Secondly, to determine if there are any other distinct interfaces, the Catté et al. algorithm is employed to analyze the reconstructed boundary and identify any local minima, indicating additional boundaries. However, the reconstruction results suggest that extremely fine-scale boundaries cannot be reliably recovered, regardless of data quality. These limitations are a direct result of the chosen cost function and require further modification to overcome. This involves applying the face and degenerate face functors, which are analogous to those used in simplicial sets, to the images of $U(m)\to U(n)$. Specifically, we define the face and degenerate face functors as follows:

- The $i$-th face functor $f_i:U(m)\to U(m-1)$ for $0\leq i\leq m$, is a restriction of the map that ignores the $i$-th element.
- The $i$-th degenerate face functor $d_i:U(m)\to U(m)$ for $0\leq i\leq m$, is a restriction of the map that sets the $i$-th element to zero.

With these functors, $U$ satisfies the requirements of a simplicial object, allowing it to be called a simplicial group. This classification provides a connection between universal simplicial collections and groups, highlighting the significance of the concept in mathematics. The goal of visual relationship detection is to identify a couple's relationship and the description of their interaction. Unfortunately, a significant drawback of current models is their high error rate in accurately classifying couples' interactions, leading to misguided learning and inaccurate generalization. To address this issue, we introduce a novel metric to gauge error-prone data points called False Positives Rate (FPR), a metric that measures a model's accuracy by dividing false positives by the total samples. By aiming to reduce FPR, we develop FP-PR, a framework that minimizes the likelihood of erroneous data points by pruning unreliable relationships and re-balances the dataset to have more positive and neutral samples. As a result, the models trained using this framework demonstrate improved accuracy and faster convergence, outperforming state-of-the-art models in performance and convergence speed. By combining RDP with the existing visual relationship detection task, called Full Paradigm for Visual Relationship Detection (FP-VRD), we can gain a deeper understanding of models' weaknesses and strengths. The FP-PR framework is also applied to RDP to further improve models' performance in parsing relationships accurately. We develop a framework for measuring quantum correlations via weak measurement and show that quantum teleportation's ability to transfer unknown quantum states relies on weak measurements' capacity to quantify correlations. By examining the process of transferring mixed states, we derive a method for estimating the quantum correlation price (QCP) - a measure of quantum correlations - in mixed states. Furthermore, we prove that the QCP is an optimal measure of quantum correlations, outperforming previous measures such as entanglement fidelity and relative entropy. We then demonstrate that the QCP's rate of change is linked to Fano entropy and show that it remains non-positive in legitimate quantum processes, thereby serving as a legitimate measure of quantum correlations. In contrast to entanglement fidelity, the QCP offers a more nuanced understanding of quantum correlations' transfer, revealing that its value may increase during quantum teleportation even when entanglement fidelity decreases. Moreover, we prove that the QCP is a more effective tool for characterizing no-signaling resources and that it remains non-negative in no-signaling processes. We then apply our framework to study a range of phenomena, including the transmission of classical and quantum information via channels with finite input and output dimensions, and demonstrate that quantum correlations' transfer can be quantified via the QCP even in the absence of entanglement. We thereby resolve previously conjectured results and provide a more detailed understanding of quantum correlations' behavior. Finally, we prove a more general version of our initial result and show that the QCP's rate of change is linked to Fano entropy in any complete measurement process. In contrast to previous measures such as entanglement fidelity and relative entropy, the QCP offers a more comprehensive understanding of quantum correlations, including the quantum correlation price (QCP) and the relative correlation price (RCP). To address this limitation, we introduce the Dynamic Graph Communication Passing Network (DGCPN), a neural network architecture designed to effectively harness communication in vision-related applications. This research presents a novel class of LCD codes constructed using group rings and a new framework for Reversible LCM codes, which can be obtained from group LCD codes in a way similar to standard LCM codes. The paper calculates the minimum distance of these Reversible LCM codes and provides a method for determining their existence using binary pyramidal matrices. Additionally, the paper illustrates a method for constructing group LCD codes using group function fields and showcases specific examples of these codes with superior performance in binary erasure correction. Furthermore, the paper proposes an approach for evaluating the reversible performance of LCM codes, which can be used to create a database of high-performance reversible LCM codes. This research aims to address the challenge of developing error-control codes that can efficiently correct errors while maintaining a high rate of information transmission. The developed group LCD codes and reversible LCM codes serve as examples of such codes, which are expected to perform well in binary erasure correction due to their low error probability and high information transmission rate. The paper provides a database of these codes, which can be used for practical applications in the future. The results of this research will be useful for developers working on low-density parity-check (LDPC) and turbo codes, which are currently widely used due to their excellent performance in error correction; however, they lack a high information transmission rate, which is essential for efficient communication systems. The existence of these group LCD codes, which can also be classified as LDPC codes, or group turbo codes, reveals that these existing codes also possess reversible properties, which could have been leveraged to achieve a high information transmission rate in addition to their existing error correction capabilities. framework and a computational tool. We demonstrate a method to apply this
concept to the geometric topological analysis of finite simplicial complexes,
representing a combinatorial equivalent. We then express Feynman integrals as
a specific type of geometric integral on the differential shapes of a complex
derived from graph expansions, thereby providing a novel and theoretical
framework for geometric analysis. We further investigate the relationship between
Feynman integrals and geometric integrals by considering the invariance of Feynman
integrals under graph transformations, establishing a connection to the study of
differential shapes. We then develop an invariance principle that allows for the
selection of a preferred shape from a given complex, expressed through a set of
local conditions. We demonstrate a method to calculate geometric integrals by
applying the invariance principle to both a simple example and a more complex case
involved in particle physics. Finally, we discuss potential future applications
and research directions, including the analysis of differential shapes in machine
learning algorithms and the exploration of topological features in Feynman diagrams.

In this study, we utilized multi-object images with geodesic segments to investigate the information being processed by the RNNs during object categorization tasks.  We found that RNNs can effectively compute a segmentation cue to separate objects, and that this segmentation cue is highly correlated with performance in object categorization tasks.  Notably, we also observed that the RNNs tend to process objects in a sequential order, suggesting a causal relationship.  These findings indicate that the segregation of objects into distinct categories is a crucial prerequisite for effective object categorization, and that the sequential processing of objects is a valuable resource for inference in multi-object scenarios.  Overall, this study provides new insights into the information processing strategies employed by artificial neural networks in multi-object scenarios. We examine if probabilistic model-based policy search in reinforcement learning can yield robust controllers that are resistant to perturbations in reward functions. Traditional LQR methods generate optimal controllers which perform well in ideal scenarios but are highly sensitive to changes in dynamics and reward structures. In contrast, our study reveals that using probabilistic model-based policy search to find controllers which minimize risk can result in more resilient control strategies. We develop a framework for measuring the robustness of controllers in uncertain reward scenarios and identify a critical threshold where using the expected reward structure in policy search may actually improve robustness. These findings are supported by numerical examples in multiple scenarios. Additionally, we propose a method for generating more robust controllers by leveraging the statistical properties of state-action distributions to estimate the upper bound of the risk-return trade-off. This approach allows for the efficient discovery of robust controllers in high-dimensional systems. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through numerical evaluations. Overall, our research suggests that probabilistic model-based policy search can be an invaluable tool for generating robust controllers, particularly in complex systems where safety-critical performance is a top priority. With ongoing advancements in RL, we anticipate that training controllers to operate well in a range of possible reward scenarios may become a standard technique for developing more resilient systems. Given the widespread adoption of RL controllers in safety-critical applications such as human automation and autonomous driving, this research holds significant practical implications for ensuring the long-term safety and robustness of these systems.

The resulting Hamiltonian is analyzed in terms of number nonconservation and the emergence of a ground state collapse, leading to long-term stability in two-dimensional configurations, resulting from an equilibrium between nonlinear interactions and harmonic confinement. In three-dimensional configurations, however, the typical ground state becomes unstable as it undergoes long-term oscillations due to noninteger periods. We derive exact solutions for two-body number nonconservation states, expressing the probability of finding exactly two bosons as a sum over degenerate states, and find this probability to be maximized in two-dimensional configurations. Additionally, we apply similar analysis to a modified model incorporating nonlinear interactions, revealing a combination of nonlinear interactions and harmonic confinement that yields long-term stable states, including a limited period of stability in three-dimensional configurations. The resulting behavior is compared to real-world experiments involving ultracold Bose-Einstein condensates. Based on current technological capabilities, we suggest a feasible experiment to measure the probability of finding exactly two bosons in a two-dimensional condensate, focused on accurately determining the associated decay rate by repeating the measurement multiple times. The resulting outcomes could provide valuable support for the verification of second-order gravitational effects in quantum mechanics. Finally, we suggest exploring the application of nonlinear quantum operators to other quantum systems, potentially involving fermions, where analogous research could lead to significant breakthroughs in our understanding of quantum mechanics, particularly in relation to long-term stable states and the associated decay rates that emerge due to gravitational effects. In 1947, Turan inquired whether a combinatorial proof could exist for the assertion that every 3-partite graph with n vertices contains at least n^3/4 tetrahedrons. (A tetrahedron in a 3-partite graph constitutes a set consisting of a vertex from each of the respective parts and a resulting structure of four vertices.) In the sixties, Ruzsa and Furedi discovered that every 3-partite graph with n vertices contains at least n^3/13 tetrahedrons, leading to the question of whether a stronger proof could be found that yields n^3/13 could be replaced by n^3/14, a bound that had been shown to be achievable by constructions based on pseudorandomness.

In the current work, a new approach has been found which differs from prior methods of establishing extremal configurations. By examining a particular parameter that quantifies the level of irregularity present in the graph's structure, it has been possible to establish that every 3-partite graph with n vertices contains at least n^3/13 tetrahedrons. Although this method falls short of the desired 14/13 bound, it has the advantage of providing a more general extremal value, a more flexible threshold value, and related results for other related-combinatorial problems. Additionally, the current work has led to the establishment of several related results and future research directions. One area of research that is particularly promising is that it may be possible to extend the extremal results to more complex objects, such as hypergraphs with higher dimensions, a possibility that is supported by the results of other researchers. 

It is worth noting at this point that the current work has not addressed whether a proof can be found that is purely combinatorial in nature, a proof that would have been particularly significant given the prior results of Erdos. In the current work, the extremal results have been established by demonstrating that certain parameters, such as the maximum number of tetrahedrons that can be removed from the graph, have a least fixed value. While these results may provide some insight into the extremal behavior of the 3-partite graphs, they may not yield a purely combinatorial proof, a outcome that is consistent with the prior results of Turan. In any case, the question of whether a purely combinatorial proof can be found remains an open and important area of research that may be resolved by future research in the field.

One of the fundamental techniques in machine learning, stochastic gradient descent, is a crucial algorithm for training large-scale neural networks efficiently. However, its convergence was only formally proven for specific networks with parameter tying, a phenomenon known as overparameterization. This paper presents a new proof of convergence for a more broadly applicable algorithm, the Organic Gradient Descent, which includes traditional stochastic gradient descent as a specialized case. Our analysis shows that the Organic Gradient Descent can effectively converge in certain conditions, encompassing networks with parameter overparameterization or parameter underspecification. This breakthrough opens doors for further research in understanding the requirements for deep learning to work effectively. Additionally, we demonstrate that the Organic Gradient Descent has a simpler form compared to existing algorithms, such as Adam and Momentum Stochastic Gradient Descent, and even outperforms them in experiments on simple regression tasks. This new finding sets the stage for future investigations into the role of overparameterization in generalization. The code for our research is publicly available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/alexjashanp/Organic-Gradient-Descent. This repository includes a detailed implementation of the Organic Gradient Descent algorithm, as well as the necessary code for reproducing our experimental results. Specifically, users can find the code for creating synthetic datasets in the 'data_generation' folder, the code for training models in the 'training' folder, and the code for analyzing our results in the 'analysis' folder. These resources provide a comprehensive guide for replicating our research. The current version of our code is compatible with Python 3.6 and TensorFlow 1.x, but we plan to update the repository to support Python 3.8 and TensorFlow 2.x in the future. High-energy emissions from ancient supermassive black holes can provide a unique insight into their past, specifically their compact radio source history. However, this method's effectiveness relies on having a comprehensive understanding of the cosmic evolution of such sources, which is often at odds with observations of local supermassive black holes. A significant alignment in the sky of two galaxies allows for the use of a spectral feature in one of the galaxies to precisely measure the path length of through-light from a distant galaxy, which in this case is identified as a compact radio source through multi-frequency observations. Further study of this source, utilizing data from large-scale surveys such as the SDSS and Ursa-Strine, reveals it shares several characteristics with local supermassive black hole evolution. Notably, its brightness and distance-tuned power have both increased, indicating an "extinction recession" where older sources appear dimmer than expected. This unusual behavior could be attributed to a local anomaly or by a 'youthful phase' where these sources naturally shine brighter, which in turn sheds light on the used cosmological model. Ultimately, further observation of this source, as well as others like it, is essential to resolving the uncertainty surrounding high-redshift active galaxies.

This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, using information from two different sources: lung cancer related text and Pathology image data. Current methods for time survival prediction are not effective, using a basic network architecture that combines features from different modalities. We can enhance this by leveraging the advantages of each type of data, but currently available methods fall short in this area. To resolve this issue, we present a new, multi-layered network architecture called the Lung Cancer Time Survival network (LCTSN), which effectively integrates information from both text and image datasets for more accurate survival time predictions. This method involves two key components: a text encoder that converts written information into a usable format and a custom image encoder that specializes in lung cancer pathology images to optimize performance. We tested this model using a well-established, publicly available lung cancer dataset with associated patient survival records and compared its results to those obtained with existing methods. Notably, our model produced the best outcomes, achieving a 77.1% correlation between predicted and actual survival times, surpassing the best available methods and achieving a notable improvement. Additionally, our model demonstrates exceptional robustness, with results unaffected by variations in dataset size and outperforming other methods even when trained on smaller datasets. We also conducted detailed analyses to examine how different modalities contribute to the model's performance and found that both text and image data make significant contributions to the model's accuracy. Furthermore, our model shows remarkable resilience to data imbalances in the training dataset and can effectively use information from both modalities even when presented with incomplete data. We have made the code for our model publicly available so that it can be accessed and utilized by other researchers in the field. In the future, we aim to build upon this work by incorporating additional types of lung cancer data, such as audio signals, to create an even more comprehensive data set for survival time prediction. We also plan to expand our model's capabilities to include other complex cancer types, such as breast and prostate cancer, using relevant data from those fields. Natural language state descriptions have been extensively explored in the context of Reinforcement Learning to reduce the complexity of representing large state spaces and facilitate the transfer of policies across different tasks and domains. This overview presents the progression of natural language state descriptions in RL, encompassing both written and spoken languages, and examines the methods for incorporating them into RL algorithms. Notably, the discussion focuses on the challenges posed by the incomplete and ambiguous nature of natural language state descriptions, as well as recent advancements in using them directly for state representation purposes. Additionally, the potential benefits and future research directions in this area are also discussed. Specifically, it is argued that the completion of state descriptions by incorporating additional information could mitigate potential risks and ambiguities, and key areas for future investigation have been identified. This includes developing strategies for selecting and utilizing relevant description components, designing methods for describing unseen states, and incorporating explicit description uncertainties to enhance the safety and transferability of policies. Such efforts are expected to contribute to the practical application of RL in real-world scenarios where natural language state descriptions are often employed. Several open-source code implementations are provided to replicate the methods presented in this overview, including the descriptions of 57 RL benchmarks in natural language form, to facilitate future research in this area. Please visit the associated webpage for additional information: https://natural-state-description.org/.

This work examines certain types of Lie algebras, focusing on $U(\frak h)$-free structures, which are key elements in developing the concepts of good and relatively good subalgebras within the broader framework of infinite-dimensional Lie algebras. A relatively good subalgebra is defined as a subalgebra ${\frak m}$ satisfying specific conditions that enable it to be isomorphic to a Lie algebra obtained by selecting a specific subalgebra $U({\frak m})$ within the larger Lie algebra $U({\frak h})$. Building on earlier studies by S. Sergeev and A. Ostroumov, which investigated good and relatively good subalgebras in the W1 Lie algebra, this research aims to identify $U({\frk m})$-free structures in the W1 Lie algebra and apply similar approaches to the partial differential operators algebra and the Calogero symmetry algebra. Specifically, this work characterizes the Lie algebras with a natural homomorphism from a relatively good subalgebra to the larger algebra, and uses these results to construct $U({\frk m})$-free structures in the W1 Lie algebra and other algebras, such as the partial differential operators algebra and the Calogero symmetry algebra. These findings are further applied to classify certain types of $U({\frk m})$-free algebras and manifolds. Additionally, this work explores connections between relatively good subalgebras, and the broader mathematical theories of infinite-dimensional Lie algebras and Poisson manifolds. A new approach is proposed for classifying relatively good subalgebras, which is then demonstrated through case studies of the W1 Lie algebra, the partial differential operators algebra, and the Calogero symmetry algebra. These case studies enable the derivation of key mathematical concepts, including $U({\frk m})$-free structures, relatively good subalgebras, good subalgebras, and well-distributed subalgebras. These concepts are fundamental to understanding the nature of relatively good subalgebras and $U({\frk m})$-free structures in specific Lie algebras. Ultimately, this work presents a comprehensive mathematical analysis of relatively good subalgebras and $U({\frk m})$-free structures in well-understood Lie algebras, providing valuable insights and contributing to the ongoing development of mathematical theories. Recent breakthroughs in large language models have transformed the landscape of open-domain natural language processing. This research delves into the development of a role-specific open-domain dialogue system utilizing these advanced language models, building upon the foundation laid out in the SpecList dataset. SpecList presents a novel framework for creating role-specified data by standardizing the roles of system and user, enabling the creation of specified data lists. We demonstrate that leveraging SpecList in conjunction with open-domain conversation datasets results in a robust dialogue system capable of exerting significant influence over user responses. Additionally, we investigated various system response approaches and found that a method incorporating large language models by means of list-based queries and response selection excels in accomplishing the specified goals. Moreover, we assessed the efficacy of our proposed method against multiple baseline strategies and found it to be the top-performing approach. Ultimately, our study aims to facilitate the creation of data lists for various natural language tasks and provides insights into enhancing conversation quality using large language models. The persistent energy release known as gravitational wave memory continues to support research in multiple areas, including the effects of GW memory on the gravitational wave background and the possibility of measuring it using interferometers. A key finding of past studies is that the gravitational wave background emitted by inspiralling binaries is largely unaffected by GW memory. In contrast, the present study explores the characteristics of the gravitational wave background generated by pop III binaries at distinct stages of star evolution and investigates the impact of GW memory on this background using Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. Our analysis reveals that GW memory significantly alters the spectrum of the gravitational wave background across all frequency ranges, with particular changes observed at higher frequencies. Notably, the finding that GW memory significantly alters the gravitational wave background generated by pop III binaries in the millihertz frequency band calls for a revision in prior estimates based on standard evolutionary models. In addition, we demonstrate that detecting this background with current and planned interferometers is unlikely, but that next-generation instruments may have a greater chance of doing so. Finally, we show that active supermassive black hole mergers give rise to a background intensity that is an order of magnitude higher than existing PopIII estimates in the LISA frequency band, indicating that these events should be prioritized in any subsequent studies reevaluating this background. Our work has important implications for understanding the process of star cluster formation and the search for gravitational wave memory as an innovative tool for uncovering this phenomenon. A key element in human intelligence is the ability to understand and interpret the causal relationships between actions and outcomes, allowing for the formulation of plans and predictions. A notable capability of artificial intelligence, particularly in the domains of decision theory and game theory, is the ability to model and make inferences about the intended purposes of actions, known as the signaling equilibrium, which can be modeled through a interplay of symbolic and connectionist AI approaches. We propose a novel framework, SERE, a signaling game-based model that facilitates emergent semantic exchanges between agents through a dynamic interplay of causal reasoning and signaling interactions. Causal models are represented as probabilistic structural causal models and the agents' strategies are modeled using a connectionist policy network. We show that, in a scenario involving a buyer searching for a reliable seller, SERE emerges with a signaling equilibrium where the seller's level of commitment is communicated through a sequence of credible signals to the buyer, ultimately resulting in a sale agreement being reached in a relatively low number of steps when both agents make informed decisions based on the causal model. Additionally, SERE outperforms a comparison model that uses a connectionist structural causal model in a similar setup but lacks a signaling equilibrium, thereby exhibiting better performance. We provide further analysis of the model and offer future research directions on integrating emergent semantic exchanges and signaling equilibria within connectionist structural causal models. The session-based recommendation technique is gaining prominence due to its ability to recommend items to users based on recently accessed items, without requiring extensive user and item information. Our proposed method enhances the accuracy of session-based recommendation by incorporating User and Item Rank Embeddings (URE) that capture long-term preferences across multiple sessions. URE comprises two components - User Embedding and Item Embedding - which learn user and item representations from interactive data and recommend ranked items to users, respectively. Additionally, Candidate Rank Embedding competes against mutually exclusive sets of items suggested by the Item Embedding, reducing overfitting by promoting diverse recommendations. Our model's multi-stage design enhances the accuracy of recommendations by retaining user and item context from previous sessions during training and testing. Experimental evaluation of our model on four datasets demonstrates a notable improvement in performance over existing state-of-the-art recommendations, particularly in terms of ranking metrics such as NR@10 and I@10. Our model's efficacy is further validated through the analysis of retrieved recommendations, which shows improved diversity and relevance over existing recommendations. Our model's code and datasets are available for public access at https://github.com/ChiaHer/URE_CRE.
