This study delves into the physics and computational modeling of multi-domain ferroelectric FETs, specifically addressing how the adverse capacitance effect impacts performance and reliability. A 2D MIT device simulation is developed to efficiently calculate electrostatic properties, complemented by a finite element method for evaluating domain wall influenced capacitance. Through time-dependent device simulation, it's demonstrated that an increase in adverse capacitance can cause gate voltage overshoot and reduce the effective on-state time, further exacerbating by the high operating voltage. We show that to mitigate these issues, a feed-back diode in conjunction with a gate shorts can be employed, which not only eliminates adverse capacitance effects but also enhances the device performance, now capable of achieving faster switching times, higher ON/OFF ratio, faster rise/fall times, and greater sub-threshold swing. Additionally, these devices exhibit enhanced energy efficiency, reliability and reliability-based area, outperforming conventional FeFETs. Nonetheless, the shortcoming of utilizing gate shorts for FeFET applications is also examined, suggesting that it could give rise to excessive leakage and short-circuit issues at high temperatures, ultimately degrading the device's performance and longevity. We propose an alternative design to overcome this limitation, involving a gate shorts replacement with a heating element, which effectively mitigates the adverse effects of high temperature on the device's functionality and allows the development of high-performance multi-domain FeFETs even at elevated temperatures. Specifically, it is shown that while multi-domain FeFETs exhibit exceptional performance at high temperatures, their performance is largely hindered by high temperature in space due to thermal degradation. Nonetheless, by employing both the feed-back diode and the heating element, it is possible to both overcome the limitations at low temperature in orbit and in space and to maintain satisfactory performance also at high temperatures in space. We have thus successfully identified the key design rules and principles that govern the high-performance and high-temperature operation of multi-domain FeFETs. Moreover, it is shown that while these devices can be successfully manufactured using advanced techniques such as LAM, MVLAM and LPALE, significant challenges arise from the low performance at high temperatures in space due to the insulating properties of the interface at high temperatures. However, by employing both the feed-back diode and the heating element in conjunction with monatomic gas and LALE, it is possible to both overcome the limitations and to ultimately achieve both high performance and high reliability also at high temperatures in space. In this study, we examined the minimum order of the power graph of finite nilpotent groups. We established a minimum order bound for the power graph of these groups, specifically groups with a prime-order automorphism. We also found the minimum order of the power graph for certain classes of nilpotent groups of a specific rank. If the minimum order of the power graph for nilpotent groups of a given rank is r(n), we proved that r(n) is at least n^2/4 + n, and demonstrated that this bound is tight. We also found that the minimum order of the power graph for abelian groups of a given rank is n^2/4. If the minimum order of the power graph for nilpotent 2-groups of a given rank is r_2(n), we proved that r_2(n) is at least n^2/4. We were also able to pinpoint the minimum order of the power graph for certain specific classes of groups. Notably, we found that the minimum order of the power graph for groups isomorphic to C_p x C_p is 2p^2, and that the minimum order of the power graph for groups isomorphic to D_p is p^2. Similarly, we found that the minimum order of the power graph for groups isomorphic to C_p x D_q is min(p^2, 2p(q-1)), and that the minimum order of the power graph for groups isomorphic to D_p x D_q is 2p. Recent research has led to the development of neural networks known as hosts, which can create diverse models from a single set of training data. Like a host cell taking in a virus, these hosts can be exploited by Trojan attacks that use adversarial perturbations to manipulate hosts into misleadingly predicting incorrect labels for specific target classes. Existing Trojan attacks have drawn criticism for their data-driven approach, requiring knowledge of specific target labels, which could be compromised by exposure. To address these concerns, we propose a new type of Trojan attack called Semantic Host-less Trojan Attack, which uses semantic analysis to determine target labels based on host predictions, eliminating the need for knowledge of specific target labels. This new approach offers several benefits, including increased flexibility in target selection and the ability to affect multiple target classes without restrictions. Furthermore, SHTA can be scaled up to affect entire target categories with little increased computational expense. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of SHTA in achieving both high Trojan attack success rates and minimal computational losses compared to previous approaches. Additionally, SHTA can be successfully defended using existing methods without requiring any modifications. Our source code is available at https://github.com/Chen-5513/SHTA. Our goal is to facilitate the preparation for the upcoming legacy survey telescopes by mapping the absorption lines in the nearest galaxies and by observing the spectral patterns of thousands of thousands of quasars that will be available through upcoming spectrographic surveys.

6. The research will also be essential in understanding how the spectrum of active galactic nuclei changes as the redshift increases and will be essential in understanding the composition of the early universe. 

7. The research will also be essential in understanding the composition of the cosmos and the spectrum of its constituent elements as the redshift increases.

Specifically, key experimental and theoretical findings from a recent analysis by Beck {\it et al.} (Eur. Phys. J. A {\bf 56}, 97 (2020)) are considered to outline the pathway for enhancing low-energy astrophysical $S$-factor determinations via new Threshold Hand Mirror (THM) measurements. To achieve this goal, a mirror $R$-function is calculated for the ${}^{12}{\rm C}+{}^{12}{\rm C}$ system using a semiclassical approach, and then compared with measurements obtained through a rotating canalization model. This comparison enables the determination of the required energy range for an THM cross-section for any ${}^{12}{\rm C}+{}^{12}{\rm C}$ astrophysical $S$-factor analysis. It is demonstrated that near-barrier THM measurements can be utilized to extract accurately the ${}^{12}{\rm C}+{}^{12}{\rm C}$ $S$-factor at zero-energy, thereby facilitating the contribution of {\it direct} ${}^{12}{\rm C}+{}^{12}{\rm C}$ fusion research to the ${}^{12}{\rm C}+{}^{12}{\rm C}$ fusion cross-section. Furthermore, an analysis is presented showing that a mirror $R$-function can be obtained through experimental ${}^{12}{\rm C}+{}^{16}{\rm O}$ fusion cross-section measurements, thereby highlighting the feasibility of performing low-energy astrophysical $S$-factor determinations through new THM measurements based on ${}^{16}{\rm O}$-beam experiments. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization using channel state information (CSI), outperforming traditional approaches in several studies. Nevertheless, selecting the optimal DNN architecture remains difficult due to the limited availability of theoretical guidance. In this paper, we explore how to enhance the performance of CSI-based localization by incorporating attention mechanisms into DNNs. By reducing redundant inputs, attention-assisted networks can be fine-tuned to prioritize relevant channel features for precise location estimation. Compared to baseline networks without attention, the proposed attention-assisted DNNs yield superior performance in both simulation and real-world experiments. Specifically, in a 2D localization test using simulated data, the mean absolute error (MAE) was improved by 26%, and similar gains were observed in real-world experiments. Additionally, the attention weights obtained from the network can provide valuable insights into the relative importance of different channels at various distances. As such, attention-assisted DNNs offer a more efficient and effective solution for CSI-based wireless localization. Furthermore, various attention-assisted DNN variants are presented to accommodate diverse channel propagation patterns and devices. Our source code is freely available at https://github.com/florentpuy/Attention-Assisted-CSI-localization. In future work, the proposed DNN architectures can be employed in 3D localization tasks and with other performance enhancement algorithms. In particular, the attention weights could be utilized to inform beamforming designs that prioritize channel features with high weighted importance. In this study, the attention mechanism was successfully applied to DNNs for CSI-based wireless localization, and similar approaches can be explored with other RF signal processing techniques. In conclusion, attention-assisted DNNs have the potential to significantly improve the performance of CSI-based localization systems. Extended versions of this work have been presented at IEEE ICC 2022 and IEEE WCNC 2022. This paper and its companion introduce a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics, enabling the development of diverse relational and topological semantics for both basic and more complex logics with features like fibring, separation, and prior consistency assessment. The presented methodology serves as a tool for designing and analysing various modal logic semantics and can be applied to establish relationships between previously unrelated approaches. The companion paper focuses on the category top* whose objects are topological spaces and morphisms are continuous functions, utilising top* to guide the design and analysis of the proposed semantics through categorical logic. In contrast, this paper explores an alternative approach by which we develop various modal logic semantics using the category Top of topological spaces and continuous functions without any additional structure. In particular, we examine several topological semantics for S5 using different topological spaces: (i) the classical approach with the sole S5 axiom; (ii) fibring Kripke semantics with fibre S; and (iii) adding S5 to Kripke semantics with fibre T. We identify both benefits and drawbacks in these approaches, discussing potential solutions to alleviate the observed disadvantages, before concluding with future directions. Furthermore, we outline two possible applications of our methodology: (i) reinterpreting modal logic semantics through Top; and (ii) establishing correspondence between different modal logic semantics. We begin by investigating several topological spaces for fibre S, before exploring two methods for selecting fibre T, thereby laying the groundwork for future study in this area. Specifically, we examine the category consisting of t-sets, where a t-set is a topological space with an equivalence relation that is compatible with its topology, and study how such a structure can be used to interpret S5 using fibre T. We conclude by discussing additional topological spaces for fibre T, including: (i) a space derived from Riemann surfaces; (ii) a space related to hyperbolic geometry; (iii) a space constructed as a collection of all valuations on a given field; and (iv) a space arising from the study of flows on manifolds, before proposing two possible research directions in this area. We hope that these papers will inspire the development of novel modal logic semantics to analyse specific concepts in other areas of mathematics. In 1980, Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza proposed the idea of robust edge coloring, where an edge coloring of a graph is considered robust if any two edges with the same color share at most one common vertex. They hypothesized that planar graphs require at least χ′′(G) + χ′(G) / 2 edge colors, where χ′′(G) is the maximum degree of G's dual graph and χ′(G) is G's edge chromatic number. Although this conjecture held for certain specific graphs, including cubic bipartite graphs, when p = 1, 2, or 4, we now present a counterexample disproving this theory for all p between 1 and 4. While examining edge coloring lemmas, particularly those involving K4-independent edge sets, our proof reveals an error in a 1981 Schelp statement claiming independent edges can be 2-colored. Instead, we show certain 4-regular bipartite graphs require exactly 5 edge colors and propose another hypothesis stating any 4-regular bipartite graph's robust edge coloring number is at least their maximum degree, which has so far proven true for all p = 1, 2, or 4. We introduce ShinyCOPASI, a user-friendly, interactive exploratory interface for COPASI models that can be accessed via a web browser. Built with R using CopasiR and Shiny frameworks, ShinyCOPASI enables users to run various analyses and visualize results without needing to comprehend COPASI syntax or execute the program, making it an essential tool for educational purposes and facilitating the examination of model properties and simulations in a classroom setting. In addition, ShinyCOPASI allows users to easily import and convert models from SBML formats, streamline model modifications and simulations, and share models with others, including differential equation and trajectory data, unit definitions, and pathway analysis results. Furthermore, ShinyCOPASI offers functionality for parameter estimation and sensitivity analysis. The ShinyCOPASI app is available on our website and can be accessed via a web browser by navigating to http://shiny.copasi.org/. Users can also download the ShinyCOPASI package from our website by selecting "Install extensions" on the ShinyCOPASI app page. System administrators can choose to host the ShinyCOPASI app on their institution's server by downloading the ShinyCOPASI package from our website and following the instructions provided. Additionally, ShinyCOPASI is available as a virtual Linux container on our website for easy deployment on universities' learning management systems. Citations for ShinyCOPASI can be found on our website along with user guides and FAQs. We invite users to explore ShinyCOPASI and provide feedback to improve its functionality and features. Quantifying uncertainty in machine learning models is a pressing concern, particularly in applications like data-driven science and clinical decision-making, where a model's limitations and uncertainties must be meticulously communicated. Yet, there's a notable absence of standardization in evaluating uncertainty estimation methods. To fill this gap, we develop a framework for categorizing uncertainty quantification techniques and a comprehensive benchmark test suite to assess their performance. By investigating various deep learning architectures for regression tasks in controlled settings, our systematic evaluation provides a unified platform for comparison, enabling us to determine the strengths and weaknesses of different uncertainty estimation methods. Our open-source framework, DUET, is now available for the convenience of other researchers. It allows for easy replication of our results and provides a resource for exploring, adapting, and benchmarking novel uncertainty estimation methods. Research findings indicate that ensemble-based approaches outperform individual neural networks in uncertainty estimation. However, the distinction in performance disappears when comparing their predictions for in-distribution data, highlighting the importance of cross-validation in evaluating model performance. Conversely, ensembles excel in ensembling predictions and ensembling prediction variances, but underperform in uncertainty estimation. Our research also reveals that deep ensemble models yield more accurate uncertainty estimates than parallel and sequential ensembles. Moreover, our analysis indicates that state-of-the-art uncertainty estimation methods excel in posterior density estimation but are imperfect in grounding their predictions in theoretical uncertainty formulations. To foster standardization, we propose DUET as a tool for integrating existing and developing uncertainty estimation methods within scikit-uncertainty. Moving forward, we suggest prioritizing standardization and the shared evaluation of existing and emerging uncertainty estimation methods across various domains. Ultimately, we aim to enhance the transparency and trustworthiness of machine learning model communication by clearly documenting their uncertainties and limitations. Solving large-scale Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) often presents a significant challenge, specifically when trying to find the optimal solution using methods like Value and Policy Iteration. This difficulty stems from the exponential expansion of the algorithm's workhorse, typically involving large vector operations in Bellman's equation. To tackle this issue, we propose modifying Bellman's equation through the use of imprecise arithmetic, specifically for the GMRES method, as a way to mitigate the computational limitations and make the algorithms more suitable for large-scale MDPs. By leveraging imprecise arithmetic, GMRES allows for the premature termination of iterations before convergence, still yielding a usable solution. This approach is akin to using the Residual Framework in exact arithmetic. In our experiments, we find that the premature termination of iterations leads to suboptimal solutions that are close in value to their optimal counterparts, with the degree of suboptimality directly tied to the level of termination. This relationship holds particularly true for MDPs with transition functions that can be represented as small-scale matrices, in environments that are relatively simple or Markov. In these scenarios, the suboptimality gap is found to be directly proportional to the square of the number of premature iterations, a result consistent across a range of diverse MDPs. This finding suggests the existence of a threshold below which further iterations yield minimal improvements in solution quality. Based on these results, GMRES Policy Iteration (GPI) emerges as a viable option, particularly when the resources available for computation are insufficient to run the full algorithm to completion. In our tests, GPI is found to outperform or match the performance of state-of-the-art sampling-based methods for their training times, while yielding solutions that are only marginally suboptimal. This marginal suboptimality is found across a range of diverse MDPs. Ultimately, GPI presents itself as a well-performing method worth further development and study, held up by our experimental findings. To substantiate this claim, we make available a publicly-accessible implementation of GPI at github.com/alexalexalexalex/GPI, an open-source repository for sharing the code. This source code allows for the reproduction of our results and offers a flexible framework for future research and development. To this effect, GPI can be used as a starting point for the development of new algorithms, particularly one variant where GPI is combined with ideas from continuation methods to dynamically adjust thresholds in line with solution quality. This paper examines the inverse problem of validating parameters for complex computer models based on observational data. By applying a multiple threshold estimation method in a special case, we show that incorporating data constraints through sensitivity thresholds allows these models to accurately represent data while incorporating prior knowledge, even in scenarios where the relationship between parameters becomes complex and difficult to interpret. This approach is further enhanced by utilizing a Monte Carlo technique that utilizes random sampling to simulate possible scenarios, effectively framing the inverse problem as a statistical inference through the use of credible sets. This technique has several benefits, including allowing users to specify levels of uncertainty and incorporating prior knowledge into the model while remaining independent of the model's original training data. We utilize a weather forecasting model along with historical weather data to demonstrate the efficacy of this method. Finally, we highlight the inverse problem's parallels with medical diagnosis and the commonalities between Bayesian credible sets and diagnostic reports that include phrases such as "likely" and "consistent with" illness. This framework has broad applications and can be applied to a wide range of scenarios where complex computer models are used to understand and predict observational data in various scientific and real-world contexts. Specifically, it has potential applications in climate modeling, weather forecasting, biomedicine, and engineering. This study explores the link between a model's confidence and its accuracy in the presence of unknown data sources, analyzing the properties that enable a learning algorithm to reliably adjust its output based on local queries for class labels. Our research identified specific conditions - bounded gradient, Lipschitz continuity, and strong concavity - under which local inquiries can lead to reliable, confidence-based output adjustments in the presence of adversarial sources. It was further demonstrated that convex loss functions can be optimized using similar inquiry methods, producing results comparable to those of gradient descent in terms of convergence rate. Building on these findings, a model-independent approach was developed to quantify the trustworthiness of a learning algorithm's source-dependent output adjustments. This approach was tested on four learning algorithms, including Least Mean Squares and Proximal Gradient Algorithms for square loss, and BackPropagation for a cross-entropy loss. The evaluation showed that local inquiries could significantly enhance the reliability and efficiency of these algorithms, often reaching a convergence rate similar to that of gradient descent. For the first time, alterations to jet fragmentation resulting from the interaction with a heavy nucleus are measured using high-momentum jets in Pb-Pb collisions at a 5.02 TeV collision energy. This analysis utilizes individual photons with high momentum to mark the position of high-energy quark fragmentation, and compares it to a model based on Monte Carlo simulations using pythia 6.4, which predicts the formation of jets through quark-gluon interactions and quark collisions. When pythia 6.4 is adjusted to simulate collisions involving protons only, differences in the distribution of jet fragments and their relationship are discovered, particularly in the ratio of jet fragments to the jet, which shows a rise in low-mass jet fragments and a decrease in high-mass fragments in central Pb-Pb collisions. This altered fragmentation is attributed to interactions with the quark-gluon plasma and are confirmed to occur across a wide range of jet energies by a rise in sensitivity to these effects as measured by a parameter called the jet fragmentation scaling factor in events with high-momentum transfers. This rise in sensitivity is lower than that observed in events without high-momentum photons and can be explained by the phenomenon of jet quenching that reduces the likelihood of high-energy jets and increases the ratio of low-to-high mass fragments. Finally, the data is compared to an EPPS16 model of pythia 8.1, which predicts the formation of jets through quark-gluon interactions and quark collisions in a medium with high momentum transfers, and demonstrates a general agreement between the two. However, the data also shows a discrepancy in the ratio of jet fragments and their relationship in events with high momentum transfers in Pb-Pb collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy as recorded by the ALICE collaboration. Recent research involving Apéry-type series focuses on deriving explicit formulas for various shuffling and reshuffling transformations of MZV objects such as double zeta values, harmonic sums, and colored MZFs. New, non-trivial equations are being established for different types of shuffling and reshuffling operations like Stokes and Aguglia-Mahmoud transforms. These new equations are applied to derive explicit formulas for multiple zeta function values with alternating sign patterns and higher weight. Moreover, the theory of colored MZFs is used to extend the domain of Fosters' reflection and Aguglia-Mahmoud transforms beyond the Apéry-type series space. The results are further demonstrated by applying a theorem that relates colored MZFs to specific types of lattice walks. This involves showing that certain lattice walk models can be solved using the theory of colored MZFs, an observation first noted by Enneking and Tommasi. The space of lattice walks is characterized by the absence of a monoid factor under the composition operation, a property also attributed to the Apéry space by Enneking and Tommasi. The paper culminates in a theoretical exploration of a virtual monoid, believed to be $\mathbb{Z} \times \{0,1,2,3\}$, based on the work of Tenner, Quovera and Russell. The research has further implications in the study of explicit irrationalities, shedding new light on existing problems and potentially shedding more light on open questions of the form 'irrational => transcendental?'. The findings have also prompted the creation of a public GitHub repository containing all necessary code to replicate the research, further solidifying the theory's reusable and interactive nature. The repository is based on the thesis work of Quovera and Russell, whose guidance and supervision played a crucial role in the research. The thesis in question is titled 'Lattice Walks Composed with $\mathbb{Z}$ and some Algebraic Consequences'. The project has also benefited from the guidance and supervision provided by Enneking and Tommasi. The research has also led to the development of a new area of interest, specifically in how shuffling and reshuffling operations impact different mathematical objects, an area of study expected to expand beyond the existing framework of MZVs, harmonic sums, and colored MZFs. The objects in question are expected to be part of a larger space known as the 'linarith space', a concept first introduced by Russell, Quovera and Tenner.

This paper examines the production of specific particles, including pions, kaons, protons, and $\phi$ mesons, resulting from Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV. Particle tracking over a considerable range, up to 10.9 fm, allows for a thorough examination of their creation processes. The study reveals that the production rates of these particles show a marked increase as a function of the centrality of the collisions and follow a pattern consistent with thermal equilibrium, suggesting these particles are generated through a complex interplay of processes driven by a single quark and gluon plasma. This observation is further supported by comparing the calculated ratios of particle production rates to model predictions based on a quark-gluon plasma and kinetic equilibrium. Additionally, the study investigates two possible model scenarios for describing the spatial distribution of the produced particles and finds that both models align closely with experimental data. Furthermore, the study extracts temperature and chemical potential values associated with the Xe-Xe system at three different collision centrality levels, yielding the following values: for the most peripheral collisions (20-30%), $T = 134.2 \pm 3.0$ meV and $\mu_B = 147 \pm 10$ meV; for mid-central collisions (10-20%), $T = 174.4 \pm 2.6$ meV and $\mu_B = 241 \pm 9$ meV; and for the most central collisions (0-5%), $T =  94.3 \pm 2.8$ meV and $\mu_B = 350 \pm 8$ meV. These temperature and chemical potential values are in agreement with temperature and chemical potential values previously measured in Pb-Pb systems at various collision energies. Lastly, the study demonstrates that the production rates of $\phi$ mesons show significant suppression relative to expectation, which may be attributed to the absorption of these mesons by de Sitter hadrons. This observation is consistent with the level of suppression seen in Pb-Pb systems at similar energy conditions. The study concludes by noting that the data collected during Xe-Xe collisions provides valuable insights into the quark and gluon plasma that exists within these particles. Furthermore, the data presents analytical challenges due to the complex nature of the collisions and the resulting hadronic state. We develop a novel method to produce evolution tables for parton distribution functions, which accounts for both internal and external scale variations in DGLAP equations. The effective interpolation method enables the calculation of PDFs at arbitrary Q^2 values with uncertainties directly from NNLO DGLAP operators. Furthermore, our approach is adaptable to various PDF sets and can be incorporated into existing PDF analysis without requiring significant modifications. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method using the Zbb analysis at the LHC as an example. Notably, our approach outperforms alternative methods without compromising physical constraints, resulting in more accurate predictions and stricter constraints on PDFs. Specifically, using this method, we produce evolution tables for ten distinct PDF sets, integrate under the DGLAP equations, and apply our novel formalism to the Zbb analysis at the LHC using four distinct PDF sets to highlight its advantages and accuracy. Overall, our effective interpolation method represents a reliable and precise evolution tool that can be easily incorporated into various analyses and applications. Additionally, it enables the straightforward integration of PDF constraints derived from DGLAP equations, further supplementing existing PDF fits. We provide the code used in this research to facilitate the integration of our method into widely used programs such as MCFM and MadGraph5_aMC@NLO for other analyses and applications. The dynamics of a liquid drop on a fiber influence the dynamics of the fiber itself, leading to periodic oscillations in some cases and ultimately fiber breakdown in others. This interplay can be explained through two competing effects: one supressing oscillations and instability, and another enhancing instability by reducing the energy barrier. A theoretical model combining the effects of capillarity and adhesion has been developed to investigate this phenomenon. As the liquid layer becomes thinner, adhesion dominates the dynamics, potentially lowering the energy barrier and thus facilitating instability. This models' predictions align with available experimental results. By modulating surface tensions, the effect can be observed at room temperature using optical microscopy, revealing an increased sensitivity to changes in surface tensions. This ultimately leads to a deeper comprehension of the dynamics of liquid drops on fibers. Furthermore, the conditions can be manipulated such that the fiber enters a stable oscillatory state. This oscillatory state exhibits unique characteristics, such as decreased oscillation amplitude and frequency, which are triggered by a liquid layer recession. This phenomenon can be explained by the effective mass reduction and we propose an equation to describe this effect. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of the dynamic interaction between a liquid drop and a fiber, shedding light on their mutual influence. By adjusting surface tensions within accessible ranges, the dynamics can be tailored to exhibit either destructive or constructive interference, offering potential applications in precision fiber technology. Lastly, this study provides a universal framework that connects microfission with the Rayleigh-Plateau instability, highlighting the fundamental unity behind these phenomena. This research can serve as a model to investigate similar processes in 1D semiconductor nanocrystals. In conclusion, this study offers a thorough explanation of the dynamic system consisting of a liquid drop and a fiber, shedding light on the intricate process of microfission. We introduce a groundbreaking method to solve diffusion equations with diverse initial conditions and input data. A designated memory function $\mathcal{G}$ is employed to soften the diffusion equation, allowing for precise solutions regardless of the function $f$ with support extending beyond the initial domain. A proposed operator $ \mathcal{L}_x $ facilitates the transformation of $ \mathcal{G} $ into $ \mathcal{F} $, which is then used to derive general diffusion equations. Subsequent applications demonstrate the efficacy of this method in multiple settings, including the solution of Dirichlet problems and cloning via regularized backward diffusion equations. Moreover, we show that the same memory function can solve the one-dimensional Burgers equation, thus highlighting its extensive utility. We also investigate the regularization of fractional diffusion equations and present a viable option when coupled with a suitable equilibrium problem. Throughout the paper, we use specific examples and graphical representations to showcase the outstanding performance of our proposed method. This research proposes a novel approach to recognize handwritten mathematical expressions in depth sensor data. The proposed method involves two main steps: first, generating binary image data from depth sensor information, and then applying a machine learning model to classify the binary images into mathematical expressions. The binary image generation process utilizes a segmentation technique based on the binary data's spatial characteristics, and the recognition of mathematical expressions is achieved through the analysis of the binary images' features. The effectiveness of the proposed method was demonstrated by conducting experiments using a dataset consisting of 107 unique mathematical expression classes, and the performance was evaluated on a GPU platform with up to 104 samples per class. The best accuracy was achieved with a three-layer neural network, and the results showed that the average recognition accuracy for each class was approximately 90%. However, due to the limited amount of available data, the recognition rates for some classes were below 50%. Therefore, the main challenge for further development lies in collecting more diverse writing samples to enhance the reliability of the system. The recognition rates for each class can be significantly improved with a larger dataset. Furthermore, the proposed approach can be expanded to recognize other types of symbols by collecting more extensive training data. The addition of new symbol categories will not compromise the performance of the existing classes, as the model can be updated with the new data points without overlap issues. The potential applications of this system include using a depth sensor to capture mathematical expressions in a simplified binary format, and then using a machine learning model to recognize the expressions through feature analysis. The approach can also be applied to other types of projects by adapting the segmentation technique and feature extraction methods to suit the specific project requirements. For example, the system can be modified to recognize binary strings by adjusting the feature extraction mechanism. The novelty of this research lies in the integration of machine learning with binary image generation and the application of depth sensor data to mathematical expression recognition. The key challenges in this project were first, generating high-quality binary images from depth sensor information, and second, identifying the features of the binary images that can effectively aid in expression recognition. The proposed method has several advantages over other approaches, as it can efficiently process binary images using a neural network, and the integration of machine learning has significantly enhanced the accuracy of the system. The main areas for further development involve collecting more diverse writing samples, and exploring new ways to capture the features of the binary images. This paper introduces an innovative method for generating synthetic speech durations in spoken languages, based solely on observed data and devoid of preconceptions. By creating duration profiles with median values and quantized ranges, we can model duration variability in words and phrases under different linguistic contexts. This model surpasses traditional, parameter-driven methods in accuracy, according to a comparison with state-of-the-art approaches on a large dataset of English sentences. Furthermore, our model exhibits greater efficiency, as it requires minimal data and can easily accommodate new texts and languages. Synthesized sentence durations created with this model exhibit a high level of fidelity, according to a user evaluation that included both objective and subjective metrics. These results suggest that a data-driven approach can yield superior results in modeling spoken language duration, especially when combined with data-driven speech synthesis techniques. Relevant code and data can be accessed via https://github.com/phoensius/median-durations.

Species occurrence models are crucial yet underdeveloped area of research, lacking comprehensive software solutions. To address this gap, we have developed spOccupancy, an R package that implements models for individual, multiple, and combined species presence across varying spatial scales. Built upon the intrinsic spatial capabilities of Stan for full Bayesian estimation, spOccupancy offers flexible modeling options, including autocorrelation, unstructured residuals, and influential feature analysis. With a user-friendly interface, spOccupancy enables efficient modeling of species data, even with large numbers of species, locations, and covariates. We illustrate the package's benefits through a case study and a demonstration tutorial. Furthermore, spOccupancy includes an extensive vignette that covers all its capabilities and features. The package's website at https://kurtzlab.github.io/spOccupancy/ offers additional documentation and guidance on the package's functionalities. The package currently includes models for single, multiple, and integrated species occurrences, as well as multi-species simultaneous presence models for one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, and ten target species. We plan to expand the package with more comprehensive multi-species models in the future. To capture the intrinsic variability of type Ia supernovae from time-series data, a probabilistic autoencoder was developed and trained using observed spectra. This approach uses a normalized Gaussian process to model extrinsic variability, relying on only a limited set of parameters, whereas intrinsic variability is captured by a dedicated latent variable, allowing for the identification of individual events even in datasets that are limited in size and scope. Furthermore, the method's statistical nature provides the means to accurately quantify model uncertainties, a crucial aspect for subsequent analyses. By comparing this approach to traditional methods, it was demonstrated that they exhibit comparable performance when evaluated using datasets from 2011 and 2013, including a comprehensive data release from 2016 containing 33 spectral trajectories. This approach offers the means to utilize the learned probabilistic autoencoder to distinguish between genuine host-galaxy scenarios and artificial events generated through a range of cosmological parameter values, including a scenario in which $\Delta m_{15}(B)=1.01$ and $H_0=73.2$ km/s/m. This is achieved by analyzing two key aspects: the density of latent intrinsic variability and the magnitude of spectra at a time-point of $t=16$ days, both of which exhibit correlations that are difficult to explain using cosmological scenarios. This method provides the means to perform high-dimensional intrinsic variability, offering the means to further in-depth analysis in the future. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the complex human interactions seen in everyday life, neglecting the role of group meetings in shaping disease transmission. To address this shortfall, this research presents a hypergraph model capturing the influence of various types of social interactions on disease propagation, accounting for both individual and group interactions. Through spectral analysis of this model, this thesis determines the critical thresholds for disease extinction and non-extinction within both hypergraphs and networks, derived from the spectrum of the hypergraph's zero-row matrix, and extends this method to more complex hypergraphs. As a result, this model offers a precise prediction of a disease's outcome based on the network's graph structure, providing valuable insights into the transmission of infectious diseases. To verify the validity of this model, this research presents numerical simulations modeling cholera, measles, and COVID-19 outbreaks on hypergraphs and demonstrates the accuracy of the critical threshold predictions for these diseases. Ultimately, this study offers a framework for leveraging hypergraph models and spectral analysis to understand the spread of epidemics within complex social structures. Spectral measures are proposed for evaluating the risk of future epidemics and detecting early signs of an outbreak. The work in this research may be extended by incorporating hypergraph models into existing epidemiological models to gain deeper understanding into the transmission and control of infectious diseases. Furthermore, this study presents several open research problems and potential directions for further investigation, such as generalizing the critical threshold formulas and exploring the general applicability of the spectral method to epidemiological models. To make the findings more accessible to a broader audience, this research presents an online visualization tool capturing the essence of the hypergraph model's efficacy in capturing disease transmission patterns. The tool showcases the predicted critical thresholds for various diseases and displays the influence of individual and group interactions on disease epidemiology. Additionally, this research offers perspectives on the applications and implications of the hypergraph model in real-world contexts, such as disease control and public health policy-making. Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic semiconductors, exemplified by the study of CrI$_3$, have generated significant enthusiasm due to their intriguing spin-dependent properties and their potential to revolutionize spintronics and magneto-optoelectronics. Through advanced theoretical models, researchers have delved into the band structure and spin characteristics of CrI$_3$, yet there's still a lack of comprehensive studies on how the spin texture responds to external stimuli in this type of material. Employing advanced density functional methods, a comprehensive investigation of the spin texture in a freely standing CrI$_3$ bilayer has been carried out. The results show that an in-plane magnetic polarization, resulting from interlayer anti-ferromagnetic ordering, generates a large spin Hall effect and an unusual Berry curvature distribution. The application of an electric field perpendicular to the plane causes a Rashba effect and a non-linear magnetization profile, while an electric field aligned with the plane produces a significant magnetization at edge sites and an unusual spin Hall effect. The rapid dissemination of misinformation via social media apps like WhatsApp has become a pressing global issue. One potential solution proposed by WhatsApp to mitigate this problem involves limiting the number of times a single message can be forwarded to other people. In this research, we attempt to understand the effectiveness of this strategy by modeling the spread of user content on WhatsApp as a temporal network analysis. One key metric that measures influence in this context is time-stamped message reachability, which quantifies the number of users reached by a given message over time. Our computational method to determine reachability allows us to precision-target digital countermeasures and efficiently handle large datasets, even when they include millions of users and messages. One such countermeasure, which aims to protect a user from malicious content, involves setting an optimal limit on the number of users a message can be forwarded to. By repeatedly applying this countermeasure, we find that an optimal forwarding threshold exists near the critical point of the network's eigenvalue spectrum, which accurately predicts the maximum reachability and thus the maximum influence a single message can have on the network. In our experiments using real-world datasets, we observe that this predicted critical value closely matches the peak in our simulations' results and represents the maximum possible reachability within our model. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the distribution of user content's reachability follows a symmetric pattern and that the central tendency of this data is heavily skewed towards lower reachability values. One such probability distribution, in particular, known as the generalized Pareto distribution, accurately models this behavior and effectively parametrizes the countermeasure's decision-making process. In the context of digital misinformation, our research provides a valuable insight: the optimal forwarding threshold lies within the distribution's alpha parameter, which indicates the steepness of the bell-shaped curve and thus the average number of users a single message can be forwarded to. Therefore, our findings suggest that WhatsApp's approach to limiting message forwarding may be an effective strategy in mitigating the spread of misinformation, as the predicted critical value closely matches the predicted mean reachability. One potential limitation of our model lies in its inability to account for the recency of user interactions, which may lead to inaccurate predictions of reachability and thus the effectiveness of WhatsApp's digital countermeasure. Nonetheless, our research provides a valuable framework and insight into understanding the spread of user content on WhatsApp, as well as digital misinformation in general. This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to collaboratively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data. Concurrently, clients create duplicate data sets and mask the original data with random information, only sending the masked versions and altered duplicates to the server for anonymous feedback. Our framework effectively prevents Byzantine threats and shields user identity from the server, and our experiments demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency on several datasets. Moreover, FLVoogd surpasses conventional FL baselines in achieving robust model training and significant data utility, all while maintaining client privacy. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/DeepSardar/FLVoogd.

By employing a novel statistical approach and considering various time intervals for star formation, we find that these factors significantly impact the chemical enrichment of the galaxy. Specifically, the rate of supernovae explosions and the distribution of massive stars' nucleosynthetic yields vary depending on the star formation history. Focusing on the Fe peak elements produced in these supernovae, we use an probabilistic model to constrain the timeline of starlight bursts and chemical enrichment in dwarf galaxies. This technique enables precise timing of events, indicating that low-metallicity galaxies experience rapid iron enrichment and supernovae activity shortly after the onset of starlight. In contrast, zinc enrichment develops more slowly and is primarily the result of the explosion of massive stars. The time interval between starlight onset and supernovae activity in low-metallicity galaxies is comparable to the time required for these galaxies to reach an iron abundance similar to that of the Milky Way. Specifically, this interval is approximately $110$ million years for both iron and zinc. This finding holds significant historical value, suggesting that high-energy supernovae explosions and the rapid injection of heavy elements into the interstellar medium play a crucial role in the early chemical enrichment of dwarf galaxies. While a magnetic field is necessary to observe spin-polarized carriers in the As-As configuration, they appear spontaneously in the Eu-As configuration. Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and thorough model explanations. However, they necessitate substantial computational resources for processing. The usual approach to speeding them up is model pruning, which simplifies the networks but often requires retraining the new, sparser model from scratch. End-to-end continuous pruning from the initial overfitting stage through training has yet to be effectively achieved, with most current methods failing to account for the effects of weight pruning on bias parameters, resulting in inefficient end-to-end training processes. ClickTrain addresses this limitation by providing fine-grained, architecture-preserving model pruning techniques that include the consideration of bias parameters, allowing for continuous pruning and accurate end-to-end training. It achieves this through the analysis of distribution shifts during the training process. ClickTrain thus enables the training of sparser models that retain the original network's performance while significantly reducing inference computational costs. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the exceptional performance of ClickTrain in various model pruning scenarios with minimal accuracy loss and considerable inference speed-up. It surpasses the performance of current state-of-the-art model pruning methods with a reduction rate of up to 90% for Compute, while only incurring a 0.38% accuracy drop for CodeNet. Moreover, it effectively continues the pruning process of models like MobileNetV2, ResNet50, and VGG16 across different datasets, resulting in end-to-end pruning accuracy retention with significant inference computational cost reductions. Specifically, it reduces the inference computational costs of pruned models by up to 40% with no performance loss on CIFAR-10, and by up to 32% with no performance loss on ImageNet with comparable results to complex models like BERT. Its source code is publicly available at https://github.com/alexramez/ClickTrain. The detection of gravitational waves by LIGO and VIRGO collaboration open new avenues for studying extreme physics, such as compact object mergers resulting in short gamma-ray bursts. To take advantage of this opportunity, we propose using deep learning to identify and prioritize promising events involving neutron star-black hole mergers, and to train a network to distinguish various neutron star binary merger modes, including those producing short gamma-ray bursts and long-time afterglows. Our analysis is based on the parameters of simulated merging events, and incorporates random noise to mimic real-world detection limitations, and uncertainty associated with parameter estimation. With a large dataset of 250,000 realistic simulations, we demonstrate an 95% accuracy in identifying short gamma-ray burst producing mergers using a convolutional neural network, and in distinguishing two distinct binary merger modes, and have successfully tested our approach on the gravitational wave strain data from the detection of GW190814, a neutron star-black hole merger involving a 27 solar mass black hole. The integration of our method with the gravitational wave search pipeline could significantly enhance the detection of neutron star-black hole mergers, and aid in understanding their role in producing short gamma-ray bursts. We examine whether specific models satisfy particular conditions and investigate whether these models can be reached through iterations of specific forcing methods. We also consider general properties of the model-order, including its behavior under specific types of forcing. Notably, we identify a scenario in which an infinite set of reals becomes additive with respect to another real under a specific forcing method, yet remains non-additive in the broader context. This achievement hinges on a previously overlooked distinction in the additive structure of certain sets of reals, which we establish through an explicit axiomatic description of the additive relations. Dualities between category theoretic structures offer symmetrical relationships between pairs of categories, often establishing equivalences between objects in one category and duality-defined objects in another. This paper explores duality theories in algebraic structures, highlighting a particular type of duality that preserves morphisms, and using this type to redefine homological properties in a dually equivalent framework. Specifically, we examine finite presentation duality for rings and apply it to understand nilpotency and semiprime properties. Additionally, we define a duality-based counterpart to the Invariant Rank Nullity Theorem, and use this result to prove a duality-preserving version of the theorem. This approach also enables us to redefine polynomial rings and field extensions in a dually equivalent framework. Furthermore, exploring duality theories inspires new contributions to category theory, particularly in the areas of reflection, inclusion, and conservative localization. These concepts are then utilized to prove a duality-based counterpart to the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra. The paper ultimately concludes by speculating on potential future research avenues in this area. The material presented here is intended for advanced undergraduate students and early graduate students. Several exercises are included to reinforce key concepts and help students appreciate the beauty of duality theories. The material can serve as a standalone course for advanced undergraduate students and as a brief introduction for early graduate students. The paper's content is largely self-contained, with brief introductions to necessary background concepts and duality theories provided in Chapters 1-3, with the remaining content organized according to the recommended course outline provided below. The paper can be divided into 11 self-contained sections, starting with an abstract and introduction, followed by a comprehensive bibliography, and concluding with a list of recommended further readings. The structure of the paper is designed to facilitate flexible teaching approaches. The level of the material can be adjusted based on the class's needs, and key concepts can be highlighted for quick reference. A brief synopsis of the paper is also included for further illustration. Building upon a previous study that employed the $E_8$-lattice for a quantum information processing system, this work proposes an innovative approach by incorporating complexifications of the $E_8$-lattice to develop a quantum information system that leverages contextuality. The framework consists of a set of points derived from the $E_8$-lattice in a 8-dimensional Euclidean space along with their respective dual points, enabling the exploration of context-dependent measurements. A specific configuration of 24 points in a 8-dimensional Euclidean space, corresponding to the vertices of a hypercube with an edge length of 2, is introduced as a quantum contextuality system. This system serves as a prototype for a quantum information processor that can effectively harness contextuality, thereby facilitating the realization of non-locality-based quantum information processing and, potentially, quantum computing. A detailed analysis also investigates various distributions of points in the Euclidean space, examining their impact on contextuality within the proposed system. Furthermore, this study delves into developing novel tools to identify emptiness in the contextuality polytope and identify facial points, which could hold potential in developing a quantum information processor that leverages contextuality. Additionally, a subset of 20 points in the Euclidean space, corresponding to the vertices of a regular dodecahedron with a edge length of 2, is introduced as a quantum contextuality system and is compared to an existing solid figure approach utilizing a dodecahedron for quantum contextuality system. Lastly, a comprehensive examination is conducted to identify all facial points of the polytope corresponding to the 20-point system and to develop novel tools to identify emptiness in the polytope. This research aims to develop a quantum information processor that effectively leverages contextuality using the complexification of the $E_8$-lattice as a core system. Such a device could potentially enable the practical realization of non-locality-based quantum computing by harnessing contextuality. In ecological studies, presence-absence data are frequently analyzed using multivariate techniques. Researchers often treat each species as an individual variable, but alternative methods cluster sites based on the configuration of species present at each site. Our study compares seven clustering methods that incorporate site configuration as a variable and assesses their performance using simulation and real-world data from plant communities. The methods examined include hierarchical clustering using the Jaccard distance, multi-dimensional scaling combined with hierarchical clustering, hierarchical clustering of matrix entries, latent variable modeling, Gaussian Graphical Model, Degree Corrected Gaussian Graphical Model, and a method that utilizes a nearest-neighbor approach to estimate a multivariate density function. Our results indicate that the degree corrected Gaussian graphical model and the nearest-neighbor density estimation methods perform well in simulations and on actual data, and suggest that these approaches can help researchers identify clusters of sites that share similar ecological characteristics. In recent years, salient object detection using deep learning techniques has received significant attention, but current methods often focus on optimizing their architectures without thoroughly exploring their internal structures. To address this, we propose a novel approach, where we incorporate spatial attention within existing deep learning models to enhance their internal structures and thus their performance. Specifically, we introduce the Fusion Module with Spatial Attention (FM-SA) which can be easily integrated into various deep learning models for salient object detection. By incorporating FM-SA into two leading architectures, fully convolutional neural networks and dilated convolutional neural networks, we develop the FM-SA-FCN and FM-SA-DCN models and evaluate their effectiveness on the recently released DAVIS-20 challenge. Our models exhibit exceptional performance, achieving remarkable results on various datasets, and serve as efficient and versatile solutions for salient object detection tasks. The code is available at https://github.com/zzt1997/SaFoD.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval Task 6 on Identifying Offensive Tweets leveraged a combination of BERT and Support Vector Machines to achieve a 72.1% macro-averaged F1 score in the 0-annotated training data subset. Due to time constraints, we only fine-tuned the BERT model. Our approach involved training a linear SVM to combine the BERT and BERT-dist features, which were generated by training a BERT model on the provided data. We also explored various rule-based methods, but ultimately discarded them in favor of the aforementioned strategy, submitting three submissions based on different hyperparameters. Although our strategy did not translate to a top-ranked performance in the coarse-annotated data subset, our approach did receive a nod from the organizers for being an innovative method. We achieved a macro-averaged F1 score of 58.3 in the coarse-annotated data subset. Upon review, it's been determined that a more thorough optimization of the model parameters, along with incorporating more sophisticated techniques, would be necessary to achieve a competitive score in this subset. In the fine-annotated data subset, our UM-IU@LING system performed even more poorly, submitting three entries with various hyperparameters, which earned us a macro-averaged F1 score of 46.2. A key takeaway from this experience is that pre-training a natural language understanding model on a specific dataset is crucial for achieving a competitive score in that same dataset. In the future, we plan on revisiting this task, training our models from scratch, and employing a more robust method for selecting hyperparameters. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) has been a vital capability for deciphering ancient and historical documents, although advancements in Deep Learning technologies have yet to yield comparable results for scripts with limited resources for training. A significant obstacle lies in acquiring a large, standardized dataset containing words from these scripts, which can be written in diverse languages and alphabets using a range of writing styles. We present a novel approach to creating such datasets from a single image comprising multiple scripts, eliminating the need for comprehensive word lists, instead relying on the model's ability to learn word composition. This innovation enables the expansion of trained models for scripts with limited resources, paving the way for the automatic transcription of historical documents without prior knowledge of the script. The proposed method is evaluated using the TITUS dataset containing Ogham writing and the Historical Handwritten Text from Tamil Newspapers. The results show significant improvements when standard datasets are available, however, they also highlight the challenges and potential solutions when dealing with truly resource-constrained scripts. This merge aims to mitigate a major limitation of the Monte Carlo method, specifically its restricted grid size due to computational constraints, thereby enabling a significant increase in the number of calculated points. Preliminary results indicate that the methods can be merged with minimal loss of computational resources, with substantial improvements achieved. For example, the number of calculated points increased by nearly 30, 40, and 50 for nuclei 238Pu, 260106, and 264112 with 8, 10, and 12 dimensions, respectively. Notably, the methods can be merged with little impact on relative or absolute neutron-proton ratio plots, but with noticeable effects on energy spectra and HFB eigenvalues. The most significant enhancements were found in low-lying excited levels and their corresponding spin-parity constraints. This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex regions in complex space containing non-trivial analytic circles in the boundary. Consequently, this characterizes compactness of the composition operator with a continuous symbol (limited to its closure) on the Bergman space of the polydisc. Additionally, this investigation explores connections between compactness of composition operators and the properties of a controlling function in the Bergman space of a pseudo-convex domain. Specifically, this study identifies conditions on a continuous symbol, defined on the boundary of a pseudo-convex domain, that dictate compactness of the associated composition operator in the Bergman space. Related findings are also established for the Hardy space of a bounded, convex region in complex space containing a non-trivial analytic circle in the boundary. High-performance computing on GPUs significantly benefits from utilizing CUDA threads to overlap memory access with data transfer, yet synchronization issues arise when memory allocations conflict, resulting in underperforming applications. To overcome this limitation, we introduce DynaSOAr - a highly efficient memory allocator designed for object-based programming on GPUs, ensuring seamless memory management and optimal memory access. This innovative allocator revolutionizes the development of GPU codes by incorporating a stack frame similar to that used in multi-frame techniques, enabling dynamic memory allocation and efficiently coordinating memory access through a stack-based structure. Furthermore, DynaSOAr employs a parallel framework that automatically detects and resolves memory allocation conflicts, allowing for straightforward code replication. We validated DynaSOAr's performance across a range of practical scenarios, revealing up to a 4-fold improvement in overall GPU speed when compared to existing solutions, with direct overhead varying between 1.5% and 7.5% depending on memory usage. To further accelerate the development of efficient GPU codes, we provide a comprehensive guide outlining best practices for creating high-performance parallel programs using DynaSOAr. This practical guidance is supplemented by the open-source DynaSOAr-CUDA framework, ensuring seamless integration with object-based programming on GPUs. We thoroughly examined the performance benefits and practical applications of DynaSOAr across a range of practical case studies, showcasing its substantial memory allocation performance improvements and simplified programming syntax. To further demonstrate its value, we used DynaSOAr-CUDA in a real-world example, successfully accelerating the performance of the HPC-FHE library, which now achieves a speed-up of up to 3.72 times in some operations, while also ensuring full compatibility with existing GPU codes. This extensive validation not only affirms the performance and reliability of the DynaSOAr approach, but also highlights its vast potential for further improving the efficiency and efficiency of GPU-based high-performance computing applications. We investigate the dependability of Bayesian network-based inference methods in an uncertain environment, where some network components may be unclear, and certain parameters are subject to possible variations. This uncertainty is formalized as a credal Bayesian network (CBN), a type of Bayesian network with uncertain network and parameter constraints expressed as probability distributions over relevant parameter spaces. Credal Bayesian networks can model various types of network uncertainty, including incomplete knowledge, data discrepancies, and the effects of prior distribution uncertainties. Our primary goal is to determine if a CBN-based inference method will always produce accurate results for a wide range of credible network configurations. To address this goal, we first establish a mathematical relationship between the reliability of a CBN-based inference algorithm and the satisfaction of a specific set of polynomial inequalities, parameterized by network and model specifics. Notably, this set of inequalities is defined over the variables representing possible probability values in the network, and is translated into a probabilistic logic constraint when considering a network as a probabilistic circuit. Notably, we show that traditional approximation methods cannot guarantee the reliability of a CBN-based inference method, and that a novel approach is required to establish robustness assurances. To address this challenge, we propose a pruning-based method that leverages the structure of Bayesian networks to reduce the dimensionality of the reliability verification problem. This approach involves a hybrid of symbolic and numerical solvers, and utilizes the properties of convex programming to provide a reliable approximation of the reliability bounds in high-dimensional networks. Our method can be extended for efficient computation by exploiting the network structure, and we demonstrate its effectiveness via numerical experiments involving various reliability scenarios, including incomplete knowledge, data discrepancies, and the effects of prior distribution uncertainties. Moreover, we show that our approach can be adapted for decision-making purposes under similar credal network configurations, and that a related reliability assurance problem can be tackled using our earlier work on probabilistic verification. A rate equation model is developed to describe the time-evolution of electron holes created by high-fluence X-ray pulses in materials undergoing X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy (XANES). This model builds upon earlier work, accounting for changes in the X-ray pulse intensity, contaminating photons with lower energy, and the effects of Auger decay, all within the framework of a multi-state rate equation system. This approach is recognized as a fundamental element in understanding non-linear XANES effects, particularly in cases where the X-ray pulse duration approaches or surpasses the material's electronic relaxation time. To illustrate the significance of each physical process, a comprehensive simulation was conducted in the case of nickel foil, utilizing actual X-ray pulse data from the Linac Coherent Light Source, and compared to experimental results obtained using time-resolved XANES in the hard X-ray spectroscopy beamline at SLAC National Laboratory. This model provides a versatile tool that can be easily adapted to various materials and experimental conditions by adjusting parameters to match observed experimental outcomes. Furthermore, this model serves as a crucial foundation towards achieving full photoabsorption simulation, an area where the model's developer holds expertise. An area for future research exploration is suggested, where the rate equation model is to be expanded into a full quantum mechanical model, utilizing numerical methods such as density functional theory to describe the material's electronic ground state, thereby enabling the simulation of ultra-short X-ray pulses with pulse durations in the femtosecond range. An initial outline of the approach is also provided in the present work, indicating the potential for the rate equation model to be the initial step in such a full quantum mechanical model. An open access code based on Python is provided for the model's description, enabling other researchers to utilize the model by downloading the code at https://github.com/EnriqueGonzalezDeOraa/RateEquationModel/blob/main/RateEquationsModel.py. An accompanying document is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.02875 providing a more detailed description of the model and additional simulation results. Also, an open access report is available at https://doi.org/10.21741/SLACDOG.2021.01.0001 documenting the time-resolved XANES data used in the present work and other related research. Lastly, two open access theses are available at https://doi.org/10.25781/BL9N-30879 and https://doi.org/10.25781/7H3K

This paper presents a novel integrated temperature sensor, designed using a 0.6V to 1.8V voltage range, which can function within three-dimensional (3D) stack packaging. The temperature detector consists of only three transistors and one resistor, offering high accuracy due to its internal 90nm CMOS process parameters. The temperature detector's conversion mechanism relies on the ratio of two 10-bit digital count values generated from two 5-bit latches. The entire temperature detection unit occupies a minimal area of 4$\mu$m2 and features a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, along with a 1.4{\deg}C maximum error margin. Additionally, each temperature conversion requires just 1.06nJ of power, making it an efficient choice for various BJT-based temperature sensing applications in 3D stacked systems. In particular, this temperature detector can be effectively utilized in a 3D stacked CMOS/BJT system that has been thoroughly tested and verified. The corresponding results are provided in this paper. A key design objective was achieved by optimizing the detector's design with minimal area requirements in mind. Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical systems, a common method for generating entanglement involves the spontaneous splitting of photons, resulting in two connected qubits. However, research has demonstrated that entanglement can also be produced when photons pass through a specific type of optical device, known as the quantum scissor, which modifies a signal photon without affecting the accompanying idler photon. Although the scissor appears to be an effective tool for creating entanglement, its ability to generate connected entangled pairs reliably needs to be verified. In our study, we utilize a custom-built setup to examine the properties of the quantum scissor and assess its impact on producing entangled states. By manipulating both single and dual photon interactions with the scissor, we were able to generate two distinct entangled states - specifically, the anti-symmetric and symmetric D\"uer type entanglement - which were successfully identified using the balanced linear detection method. Our research not only highlights an alternative approach for creating polarization entanglement but also showcases a novel method for producing connected entangled states, thereby expanding the range of applications for the quantum scissor in optical quantum information research. Additionally, we have developed a method to quantify entanglement that is robust and easy to use, which we refer to as the entanglement parameter $\epsilon$. This parameter not only serves as a concise indicator for entanglement but also exhibits a direct correlation with other entanglement measures, such as the concurrence $C$ and the negativity $N,$. Specifically, the relationship between $\epsilon$ and $C/N$ can be accurately described using a simple linear equation, which may provide a useful approximation for determining the concurrence and negativity given knowledge of $\epsilon$. Our research not only contributes to the understanding of entanglement metrics but also enables the evaluation of entanglement based on the \epsilon parameter, which is easily calculable using the calibration method we have developed. In particular, we have found that the idler field of the quantum scissor can be utilized to quantify the entanglement parameter $\epsilon$, effectively replacing the traditional need for both signal and idler fields in the calculation of $\epsilon$, thereby simplifying the process and making the method more practical for real-world applications. Our study presents a new approach to understanding entanglement and connectedness, which may have far-reaching implications for the field of quantum information science and optics. A digital Euclidean spanner of degree k and stretch c is a k-edge graph that embeds smoothly in R^d, where each edge's (1+c) dilation is maintained within a constant bound. Recent research using the L_1 norm established that any 3-edge graph is a (1+ε)-spanner when connected, and also a (1+ε)-Euclidean spanner as ε can approach zero. However, for higher degrees, the concept of digital Euclidean spanners remains poorly understood. Our research thoroughly examines digital Euclidean spanners for the case of two dimensions, and we make significant advancements by proving that for any k ≥ 4, there exists a constant c and a scale ε such that the condition is satisfied. Additionally, for k = 3, we pinpoint the best possible values for c and ε. Our results make use of a novel technique for approximating Hausdorff embeddings, where a set's Hausdorff distance to a smooth embedding is measured. We expect this technique to yield further influential outcomes in the field of algorithmic research. For constructing our spanners, we create new tools, including a method for smoothly embedding a set of points into R^2, where the smoothness of each point's (1+c) dilation is maintained within a constant bound. We make further advancements by proving that for any point set, there exists a graph that represents its geometry, where each edge's (1+c) dilation is maintained within a constant bound. These research findings hold potential for various future applications in algorithmic research, and we make a list of numerous questions and problems that our research generates. Ultimately, the relationship between graph theory and smooth embeddings presents numerous intriguing mysteries.

In IoT, a vast number of devices are constantly generating data, with each device possessing a distinct set of features. This abundance of data comes at a costly price and storing it all is not only financially unfeasible but also computationally burdensome. Furthermore, not all data is necessary for efficient device classification, making a certain type of feature selection task unsuitable for the unique requirements of IoT devices. To effectively classify IoT devices while minimizing computational and storage costs, we introduce an expensive feature selection method tailored to the resource-constrained devices of the IoT environment. Our approach involves a two-stage process, starting with a costly evaluation of the resource availability of various feature selection methods, followed by a sequential elimination of the least valuable features to ensure the optimal subset of features is chosen, all while ensuring real-time operation and minimal overheads. Our experimental results demonstrate the high efficiency of our feature selection method in selecting the most valuable subset of features for accurate IoT device classification at the expense of significantly reduced features, thus achieving substantial cost savings. Additionally, due to its real-time capabilities and low overheads, our method is well-suited for real-world IoT device deployments. Our contributions can be categorized into two areas. Firstly, we evaluated and analyzed the resource costs of various feature selection methods, highlighting their inefficiencies in real-world IoT device deployments. Secondly, we introduced an innovative feature selection method that excels in providing accurate class predictions while minimizing the number of features, thus achieving significant cost reductions in IoT device classifications. Our results show that our method outperforms other evaluation methods in several metrics by a considerable margin, with our feature selection method capable of achieving up to a 97\% reduction in features for accurate classifications, outperforming other evaluation methods by a considerable margin.
